activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: A Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by adding up the areas of thin rectangles, and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin.
story:
The school library had a subterranean reference section in the basement, half a floor below the main stacks, and Alexia went there on Thursdays because it was almost always empty. She spread her calculus notebook beside her biology textbook, which she had stopped actually studying two weeks earlier. Her marks had slipped after the mono, and while her body had recuperated faster than the doctor promised, her standing in biology had not. She needed the calculus unit, at least, to hold.

Mr. Bélanger had written one sentence on her last quiz, in red pencil, in his small tilted hand: you are calculating, not understanding. She had carried the words around like a stone. Calculating she could do. Understanding what the strange elongated S in his notes actually meant was something else.

Yuna found her there at four o'clock, dropped her bag on the table, and leaned over the spreadsheet glowing on Alexia's laptop. "What's all this?"

"Watch," Alexia said. She had typed the function into one cell and built columns beside it: heights, widths, rectangles. With five rectangles under the curve, the total came out coarse, wrong in a way she could see. She changed the number to fifty. The total shifted. She typed five hundred. The number in the corner settled toward something, closer and closer, like a coin rolling to a stop.

"So it's just adding rectangles," Yuna said.

"Thin ones. Look, the thinner I make them, the more of the gap gets filled in." Alexia slid the cursor down. A thousand rectangles, two thousand. The total barely moved now. "It settles. That's the whole idea. The rectangles become infinitely thin, and the sum, the Riemann sum, that's what it's called, gets closer and closer to the real area."

Yuna squinted at the column of figures. "So the integral is where it's going. Not any of the numbers you actually typed."

"Right. It's the limit. Every number I can type is a little bit wrong." Alexia heard herself say it and stopped, because the sentence had opened something she hadn't meant to open. Yuna was applying to McMaster, had a portfolio due, had a mother who checked the admissions portal every morning the way other mothers checked the weather. Yuna did not need Alexia's problems on top of her own.

Zacharie came down the stairs two at a time, holding a lacrosse stick he wasn't supposed to have in the library, and pulled out the chair across from them. "Bélanger says you failed the quiz."

"Thanks. I was there."

"He also says you're the only one in the class who might actually get the unit, instead of memorizing it." Zacharie spun the stick once and laid it flat. "So which is it?"

Alexia looked at the screen. She could tell them about the night she had typed rectangle counts into the spreadsheet until one in the morning, her mother knocking twice, the biology textbook untouched beside her, the trade she had made without deciding to make it. She could tell them that the total on the screen never reached its limit exactly, not ever, that the true value was a place you approached and never arrived at, and that she suspected this was true about more than rectangles.

"Both, probably," she said. "You can get it and still fail it."

Zacharie laughed, but Yuna didn't. Yuna pulled the laptop closer and dragged the width column down herself, watching the rectangles thin into a grey ribbon under the curve. "Do it again," she said. "Slower this time."

Alexia reached over and reset the count to five. The rectangles came back, chunky and crude, the gaps between their shoulders and the curve plain as daylight. She set her finger on the key that would halve them, and before she pressed it she looked at the ugly approximation, the thing that was wrong but visible, all edges, honest about its own coarseness. Then she pressed.

"Do you think Bélanger would let you rewrite the quiz?" Yuna asked quietly.

Alexia kept her eyes on the screen. "I think I'd get it right this time."

She halved the rectangles again, and the number in the corner moved once more toward the place it would never quite touch, while upstairs, two floors above the subterranean table, her biology textbook waited with its chapter on the boreal biome still unread, its pages crisp, its spine uncracked, the way a book looks when nothing has happened to it yet.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Chase carried the last box to his room, set it down, and heard his footsteps echo off walls that had never heard any before. Downstairs his mother was arguing with the fridge delivery men about a dented corner, her voice thin and sharp, the way it got when she was trying not to eviscerate anyone in public. He stood at his window. The backyard was a rectangle of pale sod, no fence, no tire swing, no Muhammad's garage across the alley where they had spent four summers ruining cheap guitars.

His phone buzzed. Adrianna, loquacious as always even in text: three paragraphs about the bonfire, who showed up, who left with whom, and then, at the end, a single line. You would've hated the music. Miss you anyway. He typed a reply, deleted it, typed another, and finally sent a thumbs-up, which felt like sending nothing. He put the phone face down on the windowsill.

Mr. Lawson from next door appeared at the property line holding a plate of cookies, which is how Chase learned that some neighbors still did that. He was maybe sixty, retired, and he talked while Chase's mother took the plate. "My son lived in this house before you," he said. "Built the shelf in the garage. Then he went off to school and never came back except for Christmas." He said it lightly, the way people mention weather, and walked home across his lawn.

That night Chase couldn't sleep in the empty room. Around one in the morning he found himself in the garage, flashlight in his teeth, looking at the shelf. Behind a loose board he found a spiral notebook, warped with damp, and inside a page headed with his own soon-to-be predicament: a psych paper, half-finished, with a paragraph underlined twice. He sat on the concrete floor and read it. Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale. He read it again. Nearly everyone. He'd been telling himself all summer that missing people was a defect, something Muhammad would never confess to, something Adrianna only joked about to keep it small.

He called Muhammad at eleven the next morning, after calculating the time difference twice. "You're not going to believe this," Muhammad said before Chase spoke. "Dorm assignment came. I'm three floors up from a guy from my soccer camp." Then, quieter: "It's far from home, though."

"You'll be homesick," Chase said. "Statistically."

"Oh, we're doing stats now?"

"There's this thing I read." He heard how it sounded, like a citation, and pushed on anyway. "Basically everybody away from home misses something about it. Everybody. And like twenty percent of university students, about one in five, rate their homesickness at or above the midpoint of a severity scale. It's a real scale. They measure it." Muhammad was silent long enough that Chase checked the call hadn't dropped.

"Man," Muhammad finally said, "I thought it was just me being weak." He laughed, but the laugh had a crack in it. "Adrianna's been acting like it's a joke. She packed a whole box of stuff from the diner. Like napkins. Who keeps napkins."

"So she's the twenty percent too."

"Maybe we all are, some version." Muhammad's voice steadied. "Okay. That actually helps. That's messed up, that that helps."

They talked for another hour about nothing, the kind of nothing Chase hadn't had since the moving truck, and when he hung up the garage was bright with noon light through the door he'd left open. Mr. Lawson was at the property line again, watering a strip of grass that didn't need it. Chase walked over holding the notebook.

"Your son left this," he said. "Behind the shelf. There's an unfinished paper in it."

Mr. Lawson turned off the hose. He looked at the notebook for a long moment without taking it. "He'd want you to keep it," he said. "He never finished anything back then. Drove me crazy." Then he smiled at the sky, or at something past it. "He's a professor now. Writes books about, I don't know, the brain or something. I can never keep the titles straight." He bent and picked up the nozzle he'd dropped.

Chase stood there holding the notebook of a stranger who had been homesick in this exact room and turned it into a career, and he understood both things at once without being able to make them agree: that missing home was ordinary, even measurable, and that knowing the numbers didn't tell him what his own year would weigh on any scale. He walked back through the garage and slid the notebook into his backpack, the one already packed for orientation. Then he took out his phone and texted Adrianna first, before he could edit himself.

Which napkins, he wrote. The printed ones or the plain ones?

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
The track smelled of rubber and rain that had dried into it by noon, and Riley stood at the edge of lane four with a clipboard he had borrowed from his mother and a drill he had copied out twice because the first version embarrassed him. The under-fourteens were his, technically, for six weeks while the real coach recovered from surgery, and in two sessions he had already learned that they could run but they could not pass. Every baton exchange at the zone was a small catastrophe: glacial slowdowns, aborted handoffs, a baton dropped on Tuesday so hard it bounced into the infield.

He had watched film of the last meet with Alison, who paused the footage at each exchange and tapped the screen. "They're all looking at their own hands," she said. "Every single one of them. Watch the kid in the blue singlet. He's staring at his wrist like it's going to bite him."

Riley had spent that evening doing something he rarely did, which was reading about coaching instead of just doing it. He'd found a paper by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, and it had rearranged something in his head. He typed a message to Alison at eleven that night: "i think i've been coaching them wrong. wulf found that learners improve faster when they focus on the effect of a movement, like the target, instead of their own body parts. so 'bend your wrist' is worse than 'hit your teammate's hands.' i want to redo the whole drill plan. am i crazy?" She replied with a thumbs up and "not crazy, finally useful," which from Alison was practically a sonnet.

So Thursday he began differently. He did not say "extend your arm" or "keep your elbow high," though every phrase like that climbed into his mouth out of habit. Instead he marked a strip of athletic tape across the middle of each incoming runner's palm and told the outgoing runners to slap the tape. "Don't think about your arm," he said. "Hit the tape. That's all. The tape is the whole drill."

The first three attempts were still bad. A boy named only in Riley's notes as Red Shoes hesitated at the zone, and the exchange went wrong in a way that adumbrated the whole afternoon failing, a small failure hinting at larger ones, though Riley made himself say nothing except "again." On the fourth attempt, something happened. The outgoing runner, a small kid called Ayana from his chemistry class's younger sister's year, didn't look at her hands at all. She looked at the tape, and her arm did the rest without being told, and the baton arrived without either of them breaking stride.

"Did you see that," Riley said to Alison, who was holding the stopwatch and pretending not to be invested. "She didn't think about her body once."

"That's the Wulf thing," Alison said. "Effect of the movement, not the body part. It's not just running, it's everything."

They ran the drill sixteen more times, and the improvement was not smooth. Two of the kids regressed when Riley lapsed into old language, and he caught himself saying "reach with your right hand" to one girl and saw her whole exchange stiffen immediately, like the words had switched something off. He crouched beside her and said, "Forget I said that. Just hit the tape," and the next pass was clean. It was the strangest thing he had learned all week: the same athlete, the same drill, two instructions, and only one of them worked.

Afterward, when the kids had gone and Ms. Chanthavong, the neighbour who walked her dog along the fence every evening, had stopped to watch the last ten minutes, Riley sat on the infield with his clipboard. Ms. Chanthavong asked what the tape was for, and he tried to explain the research in one sentence, badly, and then said, "It's like, the baton means the whole race to them, even though it's just this little metal thing. They're not passing a stick, they're passing the race." He heard himself and winced. "That's metonymy, I think. My English teacher would be proud."

Ms. Chanthavong laughed and said the dog had seen worse coaching, and walked on.

Riley wrote out next week's plan in the orange light, and he was honest with himself in the margin where no one else would read it: he didn't know if the tape trick would hold under race pressure, and he didn't know whether the kids who kept improving were improving because of the instruction or because someone was finally paying attention to them at all. Six weeks was not long enough to find out. He underlined "hit the tape" three times, then sat listening to the mowers somewhere beyond the fence, and finally texted Alison a photo of the plan. She wrote back, "we'll find out saturday." He looked up at the empty zone markings in lane four, the tape still stuck to his own palm where a kid had missed, and started gathering the cones.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost: the interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or investment.
story:
Madeline liked to think of herself as the responsible one, the girl who read the fine print, and she said so often enough that Heloise had started saying it for her. "Here comes the responsible one," Heloise announced when Madeline pushed through the door of the coffee shop, shaking rain off her jacket. Jayson was already installed at the corner table with three empty cups and his laptop open to a listing for a 2009 hatchback, silver, one owner, $3,900.

"It's still there," he said, turning the screen toward her. "The dealer called me back this morning."

Madeline sat down and pulled out her phone to check her bank app, which was a habit she performed the way other people cracked their knuckles. She had $4,100 in savings, a number she had repeated so many times that it felt less like a balance and more like a personality. The money sat in a savings account her mother had opened for her at fourteen, the kind that earned interest, small deposits of it arriving each month like a tide that came in whether you watched it or not.

"You should just buy it," Heloise said, stealing the lid off Jayson's fourth coffee. "You have the money."

"I have the money in the account," Madeline said. "That's different." She wasn't sure it was different, actually, but saying it made her feel like someone who knew things.

Mr. Khoury, who owned the place and had let them take the corner table every Saturday since sophomore year, came over with a rag and the particular patience of a man who had heard three years of their arguments about parking, prom, and whether Heloise's ex deserved a second chance. "What's the crisis today?"

"Madeline's buying a car with money she claims she doesn't have," Jayson said.

"I never said I don't have it." She turned the phone toward them, then turned it back, a small performance of privacy. The truth, which she did not say out loud, was that she liked the number $4,100. She liked watching it grow. Handing most of it to a dealership felt like removing a load-bearing wall just to see if the house would stand.

Heloise leaned across the table. "Then finance it. Or borrow from your mom."

"I'm not borrowing from my mom." Her mother would cajole her into weekly dinners in exchange, would turn a loan into a leash, and Madeline had seen that happen with the senior trip money two years ago and had not forgotten.

Jayson scrolled through photos of the hatchback, its hubcaps, its honestly dingy back seat. "The dealer said he'd take cash and knock the price down a little. Cash buyers get the deal."

That word, cash, sat in Madeline's chest in a way she could only describe as somatic, an actual weight under the sternum, and she wondered briefly whether she was the kind of person who could be frightened by a payment method. She was, it turned out.

She went up to the counter for a hot chocolate, mostly to think. While Mr. Khoury steamed the milk, she opened the bank app again and looked at the interest line, the small deposit from last month, and then, for the first time, at the one from the month before, and the one before that. The money earned something just by sitting there. If she pulled it out and turned it into a car, the car would not earn interest. The car would do the opposite of earning, though she wasn't crude enough to say that part out loud.

"Mr. Khoury," she said, "if you had money in a savings account, and you took it out to buy something, would you say the thing cost you more than the price?"

He handed her the cup. "I'd say you paid the price, and then you also gave up whatever the money would have earned sitting there. My economics professor called that opportunity cost. Choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative." He went back to wiping the counter, uninterested in elaborating, which was one of his better qualities.

Madeline carried the phrase back to the table like a stone she'd found on a beach. "Jayson. If I pay cash for the car, I lose the interest. The money could have kept earning in the account, and instead it becomes a hatchback with a dingy back seat."

"So finance it," Jayson said. "Pay a bit each month, keep the savings earning."

"Financing costs interest," Heloise pointed out, with the sagacity of someone who had once done a book report on a banker. "You'd pay interest to the lender instead of earning it from the bank. That's worse, probably."

"Probably," Madeline said, but she was already doing arithmetic on a napkin, badly, crossing things out. The problem was that every version of the math depended on numbers she didn't have, the loan rate, the months, whether the car would even survive her first year of college in one drivable piece. She had walked into the coffee shop believing she was decisive. The evidence was now against that belief, and she could feel her certainty about herself leaving the way heat leaves a cup.

"There's a third option," Jayson said. "I drive you to the dealership, you look at the actual car, and then you decide. You've been deciding against a photograph all morning."

"That's not a third option, that's just delaying."

"It's information," Heloise said. "Information is free. It has no cost."

"It has a cost," Madeline said, almost laughing. "It has the cost of everything I could be doing instead. That's the whole thing Mr. Khoury said. Every choice gives up the next best alternative, even choosing to look at a stupid car."

The rain had thinned to a mist. Jayson closed the laptop and stood, jingling his keys with theatrical readiness. Heloise stacked the empty cups and carried them to the bin without being asked, which was her way of voting.

Madeline looked at the napkin, at her crossed-out numbers, at the phone dark on the table with $4,100 sleeping inside it. She picked up the phone and dropped it in her jacket pocket, and then she picked up the napkin too.

"Fine," she said. "But I'm bringing this."

"We're not going to negotiate with a napkin, Madeline."

"We're not not going to."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In NLRB v. J. Weingarten (1975), the US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline.
story:
The argument started over a worksheet, which Michael thought was the most boring possible way for people to get loud. Ms. Kaminski had put a single question on the board, "Who decides what a job is worth?", and given each table a stack of photocopied newspaper clippings from the 1930s. Rylan leaned over the table before Michael had finished reading his page.

"Unions were fine then," Rylan said. "Now they just protect lazy people. My uncle's shop went under because of seniority rules."

"That's an aphorism, not an argument," Halle said. "My grandmother gets a real pension because somebody got hit over the head outside a mill in 1937. The textbook valorizes the owners and calls the workers 'labor relations problems' and I'm sick of it." She slapped her clipping down, a photo of men in aprons holding a banner that read eight hours for work, eight hours for rest.

Ms. Kaminski walked the rows without settling anything, which Michael had begun to suspect was her whole method. He copied the banner into his notebook because he liked the shape of the sentence, and under it he wrote the case name she'd put on the board as optional reading, NLRB v. J. Weingarten, 1975. He didn't read it. He had a shift at the Alpine Diner at four, and his mind was already in the dish pit, where the water was too hot and the wages too small and nobody had ever been hit over the head about either.

The Alpine had gone union two years before Michael was hired, which mostly meant a blue card in his onboarding folder and eleven dollars an hour instead of eight. The day cook, a wide quiet man everyone called Bear though it said Terrence on his badge, had been there nineteen years and cooked with an almost epicurean devotion to small things, browning the butter for the eggs, refusing to let a tomato slice touch the board twice. Michael had learned more from watching Bear than from the manager's training videos.

At six, in the middle of the dinner rush, the manager came through the kitchen door with a clipboard and said, "Terrence, my office when you've got a minute." The floor went still in a way Michael could feel through his shoes. Three plates had gone missing from inventory on Tuesday, and everyone knew it, and Bear untied his apron slowly, like a man taking off a coat before entering cold water. Michael remembered the case name on the board, and while Bear stood there he pulled the half of it he'd absorbed out of the air. He was almost sure he was remembering it right. "You can ask for a union rep," he said, quietly enough that the manager heard but the line cooks didn't have to. "Weingarten. It's unionized workers, any interview you reasonably believe could lead to discipline. 1975, Supreme Court. I can text you the whole thing."

Bear looked at him for a long second, then at the manager, who sighed and said, "Fine. I'll call Jim down." Jim was the shop steward, a part-time dishwasher from the bakery next door who kept a copy of the contract in a milk crate in his car.

Michael washed dishes with his shoulders up around his ears until Jim came through the door cracking his knuckles, and the two of them went into the office together, and the door clicked shut. Twenty minutes later Bear came out, and his face told Michael nothing, which somehow made it worse. Michael kept his eyes on the sink. It was only at closing, when Bear handed him the last rack, that the twist arrived, arriving the way twists do, sideways and casual.

"Inventory error," Bear said. "Turns out somebody entered Tuesday as Thursday. Manager called me in to apologize, and to ask if I'd take over ordering, with a bump in pay." He dried his hands slowly. "Didn't need Jim for that."

"You'd already called him," Michael said.

"Jim says that's the point. Rule doesn't care what the interview turns out to be, only what you had reason to believe walking in." Bear hung his towel on the rail and looked at Michael across the steam. "Where'd you learn that, the dish pit law school?"

Michael told him about the board, the question, Halle and the banner, Rylan and the uncle. "I still don't know who's right about the big stuff," he said. "Rylan thinks unions wreck things. Halle thinks everything decent came out of them. I mostly just know that a rule from 1975 made today fairer, and I don't know if that's the same as settling the argument."

Bear nodded as if that were a reasonable thing to carry home. "Ask your teacher if the diner gets a mention," he said, and turned off the light.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: French economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' argued that good economics must count the effects nobody sees.
story:
The clock on Ms. Kaur's shelf had a second hand that moved in small, definite jumps, and Alexia watched it while the counsellor typed. The office smelled of dry-erase marker and old coffee. On the desk between them sat a folder with Alexia's name on the tab, and inside the folder, Alexia knew, was the letter from the marine lab in Vancouver: a paid summer position, housing included, reference letters from two people she had never met but whose papers she had read twice. The deadline to accept was five o'clock today.

"You've been quiet for ten minutes," Ms. Kaur said, without looking up. "That's a record for you."

"I'm deciding."

"I can see that." Ms. Kaur turned the screen away, which was her way of giving the meeting over entirely. "So decide out loud. I'll just listen."

Alexia didn't start with Vancouver. She started with the swim club, because that was the easier thing to say. She had been training with the same coach since she was eleven, and this was the last summer he would run the programme before retiring, and the regional qualifying meet was in August. If she went to Vancouver for twelve weeks, she missed the whole final block of training. If she stayed, she swam at the meet, maybe qualified, probably didn't, and the lab offered the position to the next name on their list. She had looked it up; they always did.

"Rayan would tell you to take the lab," she said. "He's like that. He thinks everything should be optimized. He once told me our school board was a technocracy run by people who worship spreadsheets, and that feelings were a rounding error." She almost smiled. "He also owes me a coffee."

That morning, in fact, she had been at the counter of the café near school, waiting for Rayan to pay, when he pulled out his economics syllabus to check an assignment. A title on the reading list had caught her eye. "What's that one," she'd asked, pointing, and he'd read it out: "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen," an essay by the French economist Frédéric Bastiat, from 1850. "What's it mean?" she'd asked, and he'd shrugged, said only the first week of term would tell, and paid for both coffees.

She'd looked it up on her phone during fourth period. Bastiat's argument, as far as she could piece together, was that good economics has to count the effects nobody sees. Not just the broken window and the glazier who gets paid to fix it, but whatever the money would have gone to instead, the thing that never happens and therefore never gets counted. She'd read it twice, once quickly and once slowly, and then she'd put the phone face-down on her desk because Ms. Kaur's appointment was at two and she wanted to think about it before then.

"Here's my problem," Alexia said now. "Everybody keeps telling me the swim meet is the thing I'd regret losing. My mom, my coach, even Colby, and Colby doesn't care about swimming. And it's true the meet is what I can picture. I can see the pool, the blocks, the clock. Vancouver I can't see at all. It's just a name on a letterhead." She turned the folder toward her without opening it. "So if I only count what I can see, I stay. But the whole thing I'd be giving up is invisible. That's the part nobody photographs."

Ms. Kaur pulled her chair forward a little. "Is that Bastiat? That sounds like Bastiat."

"You know it?"

"First year. Go on."

Alexia opened the folder, and this was the moment she had been circling for an hour, the reason her hands had been cold since lunch. Under the letter, there was a printed email. Her own. Sent at 11:52 that morning, from the school library, before she had read a word of the essay, before the coffee, before any of this. It said, in three sentences she had drafted with terrible confidence, that she was grateful for the offer and was withdrawing to focus on her final season of competition. There had been no undo button. She had checked at least ten times, as though Gmail might change its mind.

"I already declined it," she said. The words came out flatter than she felt them. "At lunch. Before I'd really thought about what I was choosing, I chose it, because the pool was the thing I could see." She looked at the clock, which had jumped its way past two-thirty. "So now the question isn't whether to accept. It's whether to write back and say I made a mistake, and ask if the position still exists, and look desperate, and possibly ruin it anyway. Or whether I let my morning self make the decision for my afternoon self and call that commitment."

Ms. Kaur didn't reach for the folder, didn't offer the consoling arithmetic of pros and cons. She said, "It's ten to three."

"I know what time it is."

"I only mean the office staff leave at four thirty, and if you're going to use the school email before the deadline, you might want to draft it somewhere quieter than a café." She slid a pad of paper across the desk. "Also, for what it's worth, admitting a mistake doesn't exculpate you from it. It just makes it visible. Bastiat might approve."

Alexia laughed once, briefly, and uncapped the pen. She wrote, "Dear Dr. Osei," and stopped, and read over her morning email again, all three confident sentences of it, while the second hand jumped and jumped toward the top of the hour. Then she crossed out her own handwriting and started the second line.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 2 hypertension means a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher.
story:
The dentist's office smelled like fluoride and old carpet, and Samantha had been sitting in the corner chair for forty minutes with her grandmother's coat folded on her lap. Her mother was at work, so the job of driving Grandma to her crown replacement had fallen to her, and Grandma had insisted she come back past the front desk instead of waiting in the car. That was how Samantha ended up watching the dental assistant wrap the blood pressure cuff around her grandmother's arm.

"Routine before any procedure," the assistant said, pumping the cuff. The machine beeped and printed its numbers on the little screen. Samantha leaned forward. One forty-two over eighty-eight.

The assistant frowned slightly and wrote it down. "We'll need to keep an eye on this before we start. Stage two hypertension, so the dentist will want to clear it with your doctor first."

"Stage two," Grandma repeated, as if it were the second act of something.

The assistant went to find Mr. Karimi, and Samantha stared at the screen, which still glowed with the reading. Eighty-eight seemed fine to her. The top number was the one everyone talked about, but eighty-eight sounded normal, the way a temperature of 98.6 sounded normal. How could it be stage two of anything if half of it looked fine? She took out her phone and typed the numbers to Noe, who was in her biology class and liked being asked things at eleven in the morning.

Noe texted back a photograph of a page from a pamphlet she'd swiped from their own doctor's waiting room, the kind of thing she collected the way other people collected stickers. Samantha zoomed in. Under the 2017 American guideline, stage two hypertension meant a systolic reading of 140 or higher or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher. She read it twice. It was the "or" that got her. Either number, on its own, was enough. She had been averaging the two in her head, treating the reading like a grade where one bad test could be balanced by one good one, and the guideline didn't work like that at all.

"So it's like a gate with two locks," she said to Noe over text. "You only need one to be over the line."

"That's not how locks work," Noe wrote back. "But sure."

Mr. Karimi came out wiping his hands on a towel and crouched by Grandma's chair. He was the dentist, older, with reading glasses pushed up into his gray hair. He looked at the numbers, asked Grandma how she'd been sleeping, whether she'd had coffee that morning, and then said they'd recheck after the cleaning and postpone if it hadn't come down. Grandma said, "It's nothing, it's the white coat," which was the circumlocution she used for everything that happened in medical buildings, from high readings to the parking garage. It was always the building's fault, never her body's.

While the hygienist worked on Grandma behind the half-closed door, Mr. Karimi sat down across from Samantha in the waiting area. "You were reading that screen pretty hard," he said. "You're thinking about nursing?"

"Maybe. Health sciences, anyway. There's a program at the college I'm applying to." She paused, then decided to say it out loud, to test whether she actually understood. "Stage two hypertension means the top number is 140 or higher, or the bottom number is 90 or higher. Under the 2017 American guideline. Either one, by itself."

He nodded slowly. "That's exactly right. Most people average them out in their heads. Took me years to stop doing that." He rolled up his sleeve. "Want to practice? We recheck her in twenty minutes anyway. Use me as your dummy."

The cuff was heavier in her hands than she expected. She lined up the marker over the artery, the way a poster on the wall showed, and squeezed the bulb until Mr. Karimi winced. His reading came out at 126 over 78, which he pronounced boringly respectable. "Now tell me," he said, "if a patient like your grandmother wants that top number down, what do you tell her? No prescriptions. You're not a doctor yet."

Samantha thought about the pamphlet page, and about the walk she and Grandma used to take along the creek before it got too hot. "Walk most days, even just twenty minutes. Cut back on salt, the canned soup and the deli meat. More vegetables, less fried stuff." She had heard all of this from her mother for years without listening, and now it arranged itself differently, attached to an actual number on an actual screen. "It's not one big change. You titrate, kind of. A little less salt this month, a bit more walking next month, and the reading follows."

"Titrate," Mr. Karimi said, smiling. "You've been reading ahead."

When they rechecked Grandma after the cleaning, the machine printed 138 over 84. Better, but Samantha stood there knowing enough now to know it wasn't settled, that one number in one chair on one morning didn't prove anything about the month ahead, and that the coffee Grandma had definitely had, despite what she'd told Mr. Karimi, might or might not have mattered. She couldn't say which. Mr. Karimi wrote the number down anyway and said to have her doctor check it next week.

On the drive home, Grandma sat with the paper slip in her purse and didn't take it out. At the second red light, Samantha said, without looking over, "Do you want to start walking the creek again? Before it gets too hot." The light turned green. Grandma rolled down the window an inch, as if testing the air outside, and said nothing.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
The automatic doors expropriated the heat from the hallway the moment Laurie stepped through, and she stood for a second in the chill, letting her eyes adjust to the white aisles. She had walked here from school with a shopping list that was not really a shopping list: one box of latex condoms, one pamphlet on clinic testing, and enough nerve to ask a pharmacist a question out loud. Mr. Müller's health class had assigned each student a topic to teach in ten minutes on Thursday, and Laurie had drawn the short straw, or maybe the long one, on consent, contraception, and how to actually get tested for infections. She had read the handout twice. Reading, she was discovering, was different from standing in a pharmacy holding the actual objects.

She found the condoms in aisle four, between the antacids and the pregnancy tests, and turned the box over as though checking a price she already knew. The modularity of the whole thing struck her: the pharmacy was arranged in small self-contained worlds, foot care and cold relief and family planning, each shelf its own subject, as if the body itself came apart into separate departments. Her topic felt like that too, three boxes she was supposed to keep distinct. Consent was one shelf. Contraception was another. Testing a third. She was starting to suspect they belonged in the same aisle, and she could not yet say why.

"Those ones are fine," said a voice behind her. Ryan, from her bio class, holding a basket with deodorant and a bag of candy. "If you're buying them for real, I mean. If it's for Müller's assignment, he'll be impressed you brought props."

"It's for the assignment," Laurie said, and then, because she had decided on the walk over to practice saying things out loud, "I'm also getting the pamphlet from the clinic display, and I'm going to ask the pharmacist where the walk-in hours are, so I can tell the class the actual steps instead of just the website steps."

"You're going to ask the pharmacist. Here. Out loud."

"He's a professional. That's the whole point of him." She took the box off the shelf anyway and did not put it in a basket. She wanted to feel it in her hand.

The pharmacist was Mr. Müller's neighbour, apparently, because when she reached the counter he said, "You're in Josef's class, aren't you," and she admitted she was. She asked her question. He answered it plainly: the clinic two streets over took walk-ins on weekday afternoons, no appointment, testing was confidential at her age, and results came back within the week. "Nobody needs to know you went," he said, sliding a pamphlet across the counter, "including your parents if that's a concern." She wrote the address on her wrist because she had forgotten a pen, which struck her as a very sixteen-year-old thing to do.

Outside, on the low concrete wall beside the ice cream shop, Ryan sat down and peeled the candy open. "Can I ask you the thing I was going to ask on Thursday," he said, "so I don't embarrass myself in front of everyone?"

"Ask."

"In the role-play. The one Müller set at the doctor's office. There's a line in the script where the patient says she said yes earlier and then wanted to stop, and the other kid in my group keeps saying that's not how it works, that once you agree you agreed." Ryan looked at the parking lot instead of her. "Is he right?"

Laurie turned the pamphlet over in her hands. She had read the sentence in the handout and underlined it and moved on, and now she understood that she had underlined it because it was the hinge of everything, the place where the three shelves in aisle four became one aisle. "He's wrong," she said. "Consent has to be freely given, and you can withdraw it any time. Even after something's already started. Saying yes earlier doesn't lock it in."

"So the yes can just, like, expire?"

"Not expire. It's not a timer. It's more that it only exists while it's being given." She heard herself say it and thought, did I just make that up, or did I read it? She could not remember, and she let the not-knowing sit there instead of papering over it. "The script kid should say that the patient changed her mind and that's the whole answer. You don't need a reason to withdraw it, you just need to say so, and the other person stops. That's it. That's the whole scene."

Ryan chewed his candy thoughtfully. "Then what does the doctor even say?"

"Maybe the doctor says nothing. Maybe the doctor just believes her." Laurie stood up, and the box in her hand made a faint crinkling sound against the pamphlet. She thought about Thursday, about the ten minutes, about how she would line up the condoms and the pamphlet and the clinic address on the desk and let the class see that they were not separate topics but one continuous thing, a system, a tectonic arrangement of things people owed each other and things they could get for themselves. She did not have a closing line for her presentation yet. She had the feeling there was a question she should end on instead of an answer, and she did not know what the question was.

"I'm going back in," she said. "I want to ask him whether the condoms work with the pamphlet's clinic as a refill source, or whether that's a separate pharmacy thing. Also I'm buying you ice cream, because you just gave me my Thursday."

"You're buying me ice cream because I argued with Tanner in advance?"

"You argued with him in advance," Laurie said, pushing open the door, back into the cold and the white aisles. "That's the assignment, honestly. That's most of it."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
Mr. Ortiz had written two questions on the board before the bell finished ringing, and Andrew copied them into his notebook without enthusiasm: What does the text notice? Whose interests does it serve? Below that, a page number from Pride and Prejudice, and the instruction to bring either a feminist or a Marxist lens, not both, and to be ready to defend the choice.

The problem was that Andrew had not finished the chapter, and the seminar was third period, and he had promised his mother he would drive his brother to hockey that morning, which had eaten the study hall he'd been counting on. He found Lina at her locker with the paperback already bristling with sticky tabs, which was her way of announcing she had done the reading twice.

"Give me the crash course," he said. "Feminist or Marxist. Which is easier to fake?"

Lina closed her locker. "Neither, that's the point. But sit with me at lunch and I'll disabuse you of the idea that anyone in this book is free to do anything."

At lunch, in the corner of the cafeteria that smelled of fries and floor wax, she flipped to the passage Mr. Ortiz had flagged, the one where Mrs. Bennet goes on about marrying off her daughters. "Everyone reads her as an idiot," Lina said. "My cousin called her a gold digger with five heads." She tapped the margin, where she had written a single word in pencil: entail. "Here's the thing. The Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr. Collins. So none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home."

Andrew stopped chewing. "None of them? Even though he has five kids?"

"Even though. It all goes to this Collins guy, a cousin they've never met. So when Mrs. Bennet runs around trying to get the girls married, she's not being ridiculous. She's being rational. If Mr. Bennet dies, they're out of the house."

Andrew looked at his own copy of the book, which was still in his bag, and did not take it out. He had spent the bus ride that morning in a mild reverie about the dance at the end of the novel, the one in every film adaptation, and he understood now that he had been reading a different book than the one Lina was holding. "So which lens is that," he said. "It sounds like both."

"It sounds like both because it is both," Lina said. "That's the trap Mr. Ortiz set. He wants to see who picks one and then can't hold it."

Cole slid into the seat across from them with a slice of pizza folded in half. "Hold what? Is this the Austen thing? My sister says the answer is Marxism because marriage is just the property system wearing a dress." He took a bite. "I'm quoting her, don't look at me."

In third period, Mr. Ortiz, taciturn as usual during seminars, sat on the edge of his desk and let the room struggle. A girl in the second row argued that Elizabeth's refusal of Mr. Collins was the feminist reading, full stop, a woman saying no to a bad bargain. Cole countered that the refusal only mattered because the bargain existed, that the whole plot was an economy, marriage as the only career open to these women. Andrew raised his hand and heard himself say something he had not planned: "It's not just that the women can't inherit. It's that the mother is written as a fool for panicking about a real problem. The book laughs at her for understanding her own situation."

The room went quiet in the way it does when someone has said a true thing by accident. Mr. Ortiz wrote something in his binder, which he never explained.

After class, Andrew caught Lina in the hallway. "So what did I argue? Because I still don't know if that was feminist or Marxist."

"That's why he wrote it down," Lina said. "You did the thing where you used both and admitted it, which is apparently rare enough to note."

"That can't be the answer. There has to be an answer."

"Ortiz told my sister's class last year that any assignment with one right answer is a worksheet, not a seminar." She shifted her books to the other hip. "He also said he failed his own seminar in college for the same thing, but I think he made that up so people would relax."

Andrew walked to his last class still holding the paperback, which he had not opened all day. That evening, after his brother's hockey practice, he sat in the car in the driveway with the engine off and read the Mrs. Bennet passage properly, twice, with a pen. In the margin beside her scheming he wrote a question mark, and then, underneath it, the word entail, and then, after a minute, a second question mark.

His brother knocked on the window and mouthed something through the glass, probably about dinner. Andrew waved him toward the door, read the passage once more, and put the car in gear.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
story:
Alicia had spread her notes across the kitchen table with the confidence of a general deploying troops, and now the troops were deserting. Three books, two photocopies, one laptop displaying a blank document titled "French Revolution Final Essay (DRAFT!!!!)," and a mug of tea going cold at her elbow. Her mother kept drifting through the kitchen on invented errands, and on the third pass Alicia said, without looking up, "You can just sit down, you know."

"I'm peeling an orange," her mother said, peeling no orange.

The assignment was a historiographical essay, which Mr. Paquette had explained meant tracing how historians' views of the Revolution had shifted since 1800, and which Alicia had privately begun to think of as a research project on people arguing about a dead country for two hundred years. She had the opening sentence half formed, something about how every generation rewrote the Revolution to suit itself, and it sounded, she suspected, exactly like the kind of grandiose truism Mr. Paquette circled in red pen and wrote "so what?" beside.

The doorbell rang at four. Katrina arrived first, carrying a bag of clementines and her own essay, which was already three pages long, because Katrina had a pathological need to be finished before anyone else had started. Yacine came ten minutes later with his laptop balanced on a stack of books he claimed he needed, though one was a cookbook. He wanted, he announced, to make madeleines while they worked, because his grandmother had mailed him a tin and he was going to master them before he visited her in March.

"You can't bake during a study session," Katrina said.

"Watch me," said Yacine, already opening cupboards with a nonchalant air that suggested he had never in his life been told what to do in a kitchen.

They read aloud to each other, which was the deal. Katrina's essay lionized the radical historians, calling them the first to take the Revolution seriously as a social event, and Alicia said it was good but that it read like she had picked a side in September and only collected evidence since. Katrina threw a clementine at her, which she caught, which they both pretended was unremarkable.

Then Yacine, greasing a madeleine pan with a pastry brush, read out a passage he'd flagged. "Okay, so this guy Tocqueville, in The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856. He argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy." He looked up. "Continued it. Not started it."

Alicia sat back. Her first page had said the Revolution swept away the old state and built something new, and she had been rather proud of the phrase swept away. "Wait. So the monarchy was already centralizing everything, and then the Revolution just kept going?"

"Kept going," Yacine said, licking butter off his thumb. "Same machinery, new drivers."

"That's the opposite of my whole introduction."

"It's the opposite of everyone's whole introduction," Katrina said, but her voice had gone thoughtful, which Alicia recognized as the sound of her friend's mind changing in real time, a rare and slightly alarming event. Katrina had spent a week defending the tidy story where 1789 broke absolutely with the past. Now she pulled her laptop closer and started scrolling, fast, the way she did when she smelled a better argument than her own. "My radicals look different if the state was already centralized before they got there. They're arguing about who holds it, not whether it exists."

Alicia began rewriting at the kitchen table while the smell of warm butter and lemon filled the room. Yacine's first batch of madeleines came out flat and pale, and he ate three of them standing up, declaring them structurally flawed but morally sound. She typed a sentence about how the buildings might outlast the regime that built them, though she had no idea yet whether that was true, and marked it with a question mark. Her mother finally sat down, orange in hand, and read over Alicia's shoulder, which was against house rules, and said, "That one's good. The one with the question mark."

"It might be wrong," Alicia said.

"It's honest," her mother said, and went back to her orange.

By seven the essay had a spine: the radicals, then Tocqueville's counterclaim of continuity, then the argument Katrina was now drafting about what each side needed the Revolution to mean. Alicia still didn't know what she thought about 1800 to the present, only that the argument had layers she hadn't seen that morning, and that her honest conclusion might be that the truth was somewhere she couldn't yet locate. Mr. Paquette would probably write "so what?" under that too. She decided she would answer him.

The second batch of madeleines came out perfect, domed and golden, and Yacine set the tin in the middle of the table like a trophy. Katrina took one without asking, broke it in half, and said with her mouth full, "Okay, these are better than mine would be, and I hate you."

"Second one's yours too," Yacine said, pushing the tin toward her. "Historians share."

Alicia saved the document, leaned back, and stole the last warm one from the far side of the tin.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
story:
Nicholas got his ballot from Ms. Nakamura at the table by the window, where the coffee shop's usual clutter of laptops and saucers had been pushed aside for the mock election. The senior class had voted to run it exactly like the real thing, she had said, right down to the scan sheets, because democracy was not something a civics unit could inculcate through worksheets alone. He carried the ballot to a corner booth, where Matthieu was already bent over his own sheet, pencil hovering like a surgeon who distrusted the patient.

The booth smelled of cinnamon and burnt espresso, and Nicholas found that grounding, the ordinariness of it. He read the first contest, school board representative, one choice allowed, and darkened a bubble with the special pen Ms. Nakamura had handed out. Then he reached the second contest, the district measure about later start times, and stalled. He had spent two weeks going back and forth on it, partly because his mother argued one way at dinner and partly because Cindy had argued the other way in a group chat, her messages unusually incisive for someone typing with her thumb.

He noticed, as he hesitated, how easy it would be to ruin the whole thing. His pen drifted toward one bubble and then, in a small spasm of indecision, began to move toward the second bubble in the same contest, as if marking both could average his two minds into one answer. He caught himself with the pen tip a millimeter from the paper. Something tugged at his memory, a flyer he had read while waiting in line, the kind of plain print you skim and then suddenly need. It had used a word he had never seen before an election, and he turned in the booth and squinted across the room at the poster taped to the espresso machine.

"You're staring at the menu board," Matthieu said, leaning over the back of his seat. "You've been on that measure for ten minutes. The line for the scanner is getting long and I want a muffin first."

"Hang on." Nicholas crossed the room, past a toddler dismantling a packet of sugar, and stood in front of the poster. There it was, in the same blocky font as the instructions. Overvote. "Hey," he said, reading it again to be sure. "It's called an overvote. That's what happens when you mark more choices than a contest allows, and then your vote is not counted for that contest." He said it aloud partly for Matthieu and partly to lodge it somewhere in his own consciousness, because the word felt like a small door he had almost walked past.

"So don't mark two bubbles," Matthieu said. "Got it. Muffin?"

"It's not just don't mark two. It's that the machine doesn't ask you which one you meant. It doesn't count it at all." Nicholas walked back slowly, the ballot flat in his palm like something that had become heavier. "I almost did it. On the measure. Not because I wanted to cheat, just because I honestly wanted both." He laughed a little, and then didn't, because the laugh had somewhere in it the shape of a question he could not finish: what was a person supposed to do with a preference that split down the middle?

Cindy appeared beside their booth with a completed ballot and a cup of hot chocolate she had clearly bought to celebrate her own decisiveness. "Measure?" she asked. "You're for it, obviously. You complained about the seven a.m. bus all of sophomore year."

"I did," Nicholas said. "But my mom drives past the school at four-thirty anyway for her shift, and if the start time moves she loses the ride she arranged with the neighbor, and she was doing that thing where she explains the logistics very calmly so you feel worse." He looked down at the blank bubbles. "Both of you are right, is the problem. That's what nobody tells you. You line up the arguments and they don't cancel out, they just both stand there."

Cindy sipped her chocolate and watched him with a frankness that he found both uncomfortable and useful. "So pick the one that matters more," she said. "Or flip a coin, but then it was never really your vote, was it." She drifted toward the scanner, and Matthieu followed, muffin in hand, leaving Nicholas alone with the contest and its two patient ovals.

He thought about the word again. Overvote. The system wanted a single mark, a single mind, as if a voter were a coin with only two faces and no rim. Maybe that was even fair; maybe a tally only worked if everyone agreed to be countable. He pressed the pen to one bubble and filled it in, slowly, and could not have said, in that moment, whether he was choosing or merely ending the choosing. He carried the sheet to the scanner, fed it in, and watched the small screen flash the confirmation, which told him the machine had accepted him but not, of course, whether he had been right. Behind him the espresso machine hissed, and Ms. Nakamura called out, "Next voter, line forms to the left of the pastries."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The DASH diet, short for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, was tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around her grandmother's arm until the数字 stopped climbing, and Laurence wrote down 158 over 96 on the pad she kept beside the kitchen table. The doctor had said the words at Tuesday's appointment, and her grandmother had repeated them on the drive home as if they were the name of a country she would now have to emigrate to: DASH diet. She was to follow it and come back in six weeks. That was all the doctor had time for, her grandmother said, before the nurse called the next patient.

Laurence was staying at the house for the last three weeks of summer, a stretch of liminality she had been looking forward to until it filled up with this. She set her phone on the counter and looked up the name while her grandmother rinsed lettuce at the sink. The letters stood for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It had been tested in a US trial, funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and published in 1997. She read the sentence twice. Her grandmother had been forty-nine then, running the flower stall outside the station, and no one had told her anything.

"Grandma," she said. "This diet they gave you. It's not a brand or anything. It was tested in a trial. Nineteen ninety-seven. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute paid for it." Her grandmother dried her hands on the towel and looked at the screen. "So it's old," she said. "Like me." She laughed, then stopped laughing.

They drove to the supermarket on Thursday with a list Laurence had collated from three websites, grouped by aisle so they would not have to double back. Fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy, beans, the salt substitutes her grandmother swore she would refuse. In the car her grandmother talked about a boy from Kenya who used to buy gladioli from the stall, and a woman from Lahore who took carnations every Friday, and Laurence understood that this kitchen, this street, this whole end of town, was more cosmopolitan than any campus she was about to move to. At the checkout her grandmother added a newspaper without asking, and a bag of salted peanuts that she placed on the belt with her chin slightly raised, and Laurence let it go through because it was not her house.

Theodore came by on Saturday with the blood pressure monitor his mother used, a grey box with a cuff sized for a larger arm, and showed Laurence how to seat her grandmother, back supported, feet flat, arm level with her heart. "You have to take it twice and ignore the first one," he said. "Yasser's whole family does this, that's how I know." The first reading came out 146 over 92. The second, taken three minutes later with everyone silent and the radio off, was 138 over 88. Laurence recorded both in the pad, then drew a small table with columns for morning and evening, because numbers sitting in tables felt like numbers that could change.

Her grandmother walked every day after that, down to the war memorial and back, twenty minutes at first and then thirty. Laurence went with her on the days she didn't have packing to do, and on those walks she tried out explanations, testing them the way she would have to test arguments in her first-year seminars. "The top number is the pressure when your heart beats," she said. "The bottom one is between beats. Diet and walking change them, that's what the diet was tested for." Her grandmother said, "Mm," and pointed out a house where a man had once kept peacocks.

In the fifth week they measured 132 over 84, then, two mornings later, 129 over 82. Laurence circled both numbers in green. She wanted to say the diet had done it, the walking had done it, the trial from 1997 had reached across twenty-eight years into this kitchen, and she could not say any of it with certainty. It might have been the readings themselves, scattering the way readings do. It might have been something she had not thought of. She wrote the numbers down anyway, in their columns, and left the conclusions blank.

At the follow-up appointment the nurse took her grandmother's pressure again and frowned at the screen. "It's 124 over 78," she said. "That's not what we have on file." She checked the file twice, then went to fetch the doctor, and when she came back she was holding the original chart from July. The number in the chart read 128 over 80. The 158 over 96 had never been entered. Somewhere between the exam room and the computer, someone had typed it into the wrong line, onto the wrong patient, a man two records down.

On the drive home her grandmother was quiet for the first mile. Then she said, "So I did all that for nothing." Laurence kept her eyes on the road. "I don't know," she said. "You're walking thirty minutes. You made me eat lentils for three weeks." At the traffic lights her grandmother opened the glovebox, took out the bag of salted peanuts she had kept hidden there since the supermarket, and tore the corner with her teeth.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and old paint, the particular odor of plywood sets left up too long, and Carson stood in the third row of folded seats with a photocopied script in his hand, trying to imagine the stage full of people who would do what he told them. He had auditioned for the spring one-acts every year since he was twelve and had never been cast, and when Ms. Abdi, who ran the youth program, offered him the director's chair instead, he had said yes before he understood what he was agreeing to. The play was twenty-two pages long. It had four characters and one set, a kitchen. He had two weeks.

The first rehearsal was a disaster he should have prognosticated, though in fairness nobody had told him how to see it coming. Fiona, who was playing the older sister, and Griffin, who was playing the neighbor, both arrived with their lines half-memorized and their own firm ideas about where to stand. Carson let them wander where they liked because he didn't want to be the seventeen-year-old telling people where to go. By the end of the night, in scene two, Fiona crossed left while Griffin crossed right, they collided near the imaginary refrigerator, and Fiona stepped back into the fake stove, which wobbled on its unfinished legs.

"Sorry," Griffin said, steadying the stove. "Whose call is that, though? Where we're supposed to be?"

Carson said he'd figure it out by Thursday. He said it with more confidence than he had.

At home he spread the script across the kitchen table and found his mother's pencil, the one she kept for filling out the remittance slip for the water bill, still sharp. He did not know the word for what he was missing, so he drew the stage instead: a rectangle, the kitchen drawn in from the copy of the ground plan Ms. Abdi had given him, arrows where people ought to move. He noticed, in the quiet of the dining room, that the script told him almost nothing about bodies. It told him what people said. Everything else, the crossing and the standing and the sitting and the turning away, was his to decide, and it would be set during rehearsals, by him, movement by movement. He worked until eleven, sketching arrows, erasing them, sketching new ones, and by the end he had scene one mapped like a small city.

The word he needed he got from Fiona, of all people, who had done a workshop the previous summer. "You mean blocking," she said on Thursday, when he showed her the pencil drawings. "My workshop teacher called it that. Blocking. Where everyone stands and moves." She looked at his arrows and raised an eyebrow. "You did all this?"

"Mostly between ten and midnight," Carson said.

They ran scene two with the new plan. Griffin entered downstage right, Fiona moved upstage to the sink before he spoke, and where the collision had been there was now a clean cross, Fiona sliding behind the table while Griffin took her old spot by the stove. The scene breathed. The dialogue, which had sounded flat on Tuesday, suddenly had a geometry to it, the sister busy with dishes while the neighbor circled closer, and Carson felt something settle in his chest that he hadn't known was lifted.

But by Saturday he understood he had traded one problem for another. The blocking was his, but the actors kept improving it, or trying to. Griffin wanted to sit for the whole confession monologue; Carson wanted him standing. Fiona argued that her cross to the window in scene three felt unnatural, and she was right, it did, and he had drawn it anyway because the arrow looked tidy on paper. He sat in the dark house during their break and looked at the stage, the mopped floor still holding the faint alluvial sweep of a flood from a show two seasons ago, the water line visible under the lights, and he thought about the difference between deciding and dictating. His diagrams were a plan, not the plan. He had read somewhere that the director's job was to have opinions strong enough to be obeyed and loose enough to be wrong, and he hadn't understood the sentence until this exact moment, sitting in a folding seat with a pencil behind his ear.

When they came back he called them both onto the stage. "Fiona, forget the window," he said. "Show me where you'd actually go." She walked it three ways, tried a fourth, and stopped at the counter with her back half-turned, which was better than anything he had drawn. "That," Carson said. "That one. That's the blocking now." He wrote it down in the margin, in pencil, so it could still change.

Ms. Abdi watched the last run from the back row with her arms folded, and afterward she told him the pacing in scene four needed tightening and that the stove still wobbled when anyone leaned on it. Then she asked whether he wanted to direct again next season. Carson looked at the stage, at the taped marks on the floor where Fiona and Griffin would stand tomorrow, at his own pencil arrows already half erased and redrawn, and said, "Ask me after opening night."

"Fair enough," she said, and handed him the spare roll of gaffer tape.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
Katherine spread the newspaper on the kitchen table and pinned the corners with salt shaker and mug, as if it might blow away and take her grade with it. Tomorrow morning, in Ms. Morales's class, she had to read a short Arabic article aloud and summarise it in English, and she had chosen this one, about a coastal town's flooded market, because her grandmother used to talk about markets like that. She set her phone timer for six minutes, the length Ms. Morales had given them, and began.

The first sentence stopped her cold. She could sound out every letter, but the words her mouth made were not the words her grandmother had made. Where Sitti would have said "esh hada," the page said "ma hadha," stiff and formal, like a man in a suit standing where a neighbour should be. Katherine read it twice, three times, and the timer ticked through a full minute while she sat with her hand flat on the paper.

Rachel texted a photo of her own article, in Spanish, with the caption "mine's about a soccer match, lucky me." Then a second message: "come over later? my mom's asking if you'll stay for dinner. she wants to talk to you about the youth group thing." Katherine looked at that for a while. Rachel's mother ran the youth group at their church and had been gently recruiting her since September, and Rachel wanted backup at the table, someone to deflect the invitation with a laugh. Katherine typed "maybe after I get this done," which was true and also a small delay, because she could not yet tell Rachel whether she would say yes if asked directly.

She called her grandmother, who was peeling potatoes in her own kitchen two neighbourhoods away. "Read it to me," Sitti said, so Katherine read the first paragraph down the phone, slow and careful, and heard her grandmother's silence before she heard her laugh. "That's newspaper talk," Sitti said. "That's how they write it everywhere, in all the countries. Not how anybody talks." Katherine asked what she meant, everywhere, and Sitti said, "The papers in Egypt, the papers in Lebanon, my cousin's paper in Jordan, all the same kind of Arabic on the page. We each read it in our own accent at home, but the writing is one writing." Katherine wrote none of this down, because she was too busy noticing that she understood it already, the way you recognise a face before you can name it.

She went back to the article with the timer reset. The vocabulary was different from Sitti's kitchen, but the grammar held still under it, and she found that if she stopped translating word by word and let the sentence carry her, she could follow the flood story the way she followed the news in English: a market flooded, vendors losing a season's stock, a promise from an official that the water would be pumped by Friday. When the timer rang she gave the summary aloud to the empty kitchen, and the sound of her own voice saying it in English startled her, because it was good.

Still, an honest part of her stayed uncertain, and she let it stay. She could read the article, but she could not yet hear in it the particular music her grandmother made when she spoke, and she did not know whether tomorrow, reading aloud, she should use the page's stiff words exactly as written or let her own accent seep through them the way Sitti read headlines at the kitchen table, half newspaper, half home. Ms. Morales had not said which was wanted. Katherine suspected the answer was that nobody wanted her to choose, only to notice she had.

She walked to Rachel's house in the blue evening, the folded article in her jacket pocket, going over the third paragraph, the one about the official's promise, whose grammar kept sliding out of her grip. At the table Rachel's mother asked about the youth group, light and casual, a hand already refilling Katherine's glass before Katherine answered, and Rachel kicked her gently under the table, once, twice, a small seismic event in the woodwork that meant please.

Katherine said she'd think about it, and meant it, and then turned to Rachel's mother and asked, "Did you know newspapers all across the Arabic-speaking countries use one written Arabic, not the local dialects? Same words in Egypt and Lebanon and Jordan." Rachel's mother said she did not, and leaned in, and Rachel, relieved of the recruitment for one more evening, passed Katherine the bread without being asked.

"Read me the flood one after dinner," Rachel said. "I want to hear what it sounds like."

"Like a man in a suit," Katherine said, "standing in my grandmother's kitchen."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
Zachary had walked past the elementary school a hundred times without once going in, and now that he had a reason, the doors looked smaller than he remembered. The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and coffee. A folding table held a sign-in sheet, and behind it a woman with reading glasses on a chain was explaining something to a girl whose shoulders had gone rigid.

"I'm telling you, you're not on the list," the woman said. "If you registered, you'd be here."

"I've voted before," the girl said. "Twice. I don't understand what list."

Zachary took his place in line behind her, holding his own registration card like a ticket he was afraid of losing. The girl turned around, and he recognized her from his American government class, though he couldn't place her name until she said, "You're Zachary, right? Isabel. We did the electoral college thing together in the fall."

"I remember," he said. "You drew all those swing states."

"Isabel Novak," she said to the woman at the table. "I voted in high school. In North Dakota. You just show up and show your ID."

The woman's glasses came down from their chain to her nose. "That's not how it works here, hon. Here you register first."

"There's no registering in North Dakota," Isabel said, and her voice had the careful flatness of someone repeating something she'd said too many times. "It's the only state without it. They got rid of registration back in 1951. You show identification at the polls instead."

The woman blinked and looked at her colleague, an older man assembling a privacy screen, who shrugged. "That might be," she said. "But you're in Ohio now."

Zachary stood there feeling the strange vertigo of it. He had spent a semester compartmentalizing politics into units, chapters, a series of boxes he could pass tests on, and here was a fact escaping every box. Isabel Novak had done the same civic act he was about to do, twice, with nothing but a driver's license, and the machinery of it had been entirely different. He thought of his father saying your vote matters, a platitude he'd heard so often it had worn smooth as river stone, and he had never once asked what the vote actually was, mechanically, state by state.

"Can she still vote today?" he asked.

The woman tapped a form. "Provisional ballot. She fills this out, it gets counted later if she's verified."

"Later," Isabel repeated, as if the word itself were a small insult. She took the form to a table by the bleachers, and Zachary watched her write her name twice, then sit with the pen hovering, torpid in the middle of the fluorescent light, as if the effort of proving she existed had used up whatever energy she'd brought for participating.

When his turn came, he gave his name, signed the line, and carried his ballot to a booth. Six choices. He had decided five of them weeks ago, sitting at the kitchen table with sample ballots and his phone open to three different sites, trying to cross-check claims against sources. The sixth was a county judgeship he'd barely thought about, and now, in the booth, he remembered Ms. Siddiqui, his government teacher, telling them that uncertainty was not the same as indifference, that the honest voter was not the one with no doubts but the one who knew which doubts were his. He'd rolled his eyes at the time. He did not roll his eyes now. He marked the fifth choice quickly and sat with the sixth.

Isabel was waiting outside when he came through the double doors, the cold air reviving something in her face. "Did you do it?" she asked.

"Did it. You?"

"Provisional." She held up her wrist, where she'd written a phone number in pen, the election office's, the man with the privacy screen had given it to her. "I have to call in ten days and find out if I exist in this state." She laughed, not bitterly, more like someone setting down something heavy to look at it. "I've moved four times in my life. Every time, some new rule about who I am on paper."

"That's the thing," Zachary said. "I thought voting was voting. One thing, everywhere."

"Nobody tells you it's fifty different machines." She looked back at the school. "Or forty-nine and one, I guess."

They walked toward the parking lot together, past a man carrying a folded lawn chair in from the sidewalk, past the EXIT sign glowing over the door. Zachary thought about his father's worn smooth sentence again, and about how it wasn't wrong, exactly, only incomplete, the way most true things people said turned out to be. His vote had gone into the machine here, and hers might or might not, depending on a form and a ten-day phone call, and both of those facts sat side by side without one canceling the other.

"So did you figure out the judge?" Isabel asked. "The one nobody's heard of."

"I picked," he said. "I might be wrong about him."

"Join the club," she said, and pulled her keys from her pocket.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
