knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
The message arrived on Saturday morning while Carson was still lying on the pull-out couch in his grandfather's back room, the one that smelled of cedar and old newsprint. Kassidy had sent a video with the note, "Watch my extemp before Monday? Coach says I'm drifting in the middle minute. Be honest. Actually honest." He watched it twice over his grandmother's toast: two minutes and change on water rights in the western states, strong open, strong close, and between them a stretch where she repeated herself, hedged, and looked at the floor. The honest thing to say was that the middle was bad. He typed "the middle is bad," then deleted it, then typed it again, then put the phone face down on the quilt.

His grandfather was at the kitchen table sorting envelopes. "There's one from the university," he said, sliding a check across the wood. "For the lecture I gave in March. They call it an honorarium. Forty dollars and my train fare, which tells you exactly what they think of retired geographers." Carson turned the check over in his fingers without really reading it. "You could help me with something," he said, and explained about Kassidy, and the video, and the coach's verdict, and how every draft of his reply came out either cruel or useless. His grandfather said only, "Grandmother's papers are in the study. The marked ones. Have a look, if you want."

The study shelves held forty years of student essays, boxed by decade. Carson pulled a folder at random and found a page his grandmother had graded in blue pencil, dense with corrections, and at the bottom, in her careful hand: "This is a C because I expect A work from you, and I have no doubt you can produce it." The next draft, clipped behind the first, was an A. He sat cross-legged on the floor and read half a dozen more. Some had the closing sentence and some didn't, and he noticed, slowly and without trusting himself at first, that the revised drafts clustered behind the ones with the sentence. It could have been coincidence. It could have been that she only wrote it to students she already believed in, which would mean the sentence wasn't the cause of anything.

He looked it up on his phone, half ashamed of looking, because it felt like snooping in his grandmother's method. But the search returned a 2014 study led by David Yeager, and the finding was there in plain language: students were more likely to revise essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. He read it twice. It matched what the boxes seemed to say, and it matched something the coach did too, he realized, the way she opened every teardown with "I wouldn't bother if you couldn't do this." Whether it worked because of trust or because of standards or because of some mixture the study didn't name, he couldn't tell, and he decided he didn't need to resolve that in order to use it.

He drafted the reply in the study, at his grandmother's old desk, beneath a framed photograph of a montane meadow she had taken somewhere in the Rockies, wildflowers going up past the treeline. The first sentence he wrote was "I know you can take the middle minute apart and rebuild it, because you rebuilt your open at regionals in one night." Then the specifics: at 0:47 she restated her thesis instead of advancing it; at 1:05 she used "arguably" three times in one breath; the transition to the farmers' angle arrived without a signpost, so it felt like a subject change rather than an argument. He cut anything that was just decoration, anything that said "great job" to soften what followed. He reread the whole thing once and sent it before he could make it worse.

Kassidy called him twenty minutes later. "Okay, the 0:47 thing," she said, her voice tinny against the cedar walls. "I watched it. I do that every single round and nobody ever told me. Coach just says 'drifting.'" She was quiet a second. "The first line, though. Did you mean that, or was it, like, a cushion?" He looked at the montane photograph, at the flowers climbing past where trees gave up. "I meant it," he said. "Grandmother used to write it on essays. There's actually a study. In 2014, David Yeager found students revised more when the criticism came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them." A pause on the line. "So you experiment on me?" she said, and he could hear her smiling. "Whatever. It worked. I'm rewriting the middle minute tonight. Send me anything else you notice. All of it. Don't cushion it."

They stayed on the phone while she reworked the transitions, reading lines aloud, and he offered what he could, sometimes usefully, sometimes not. Later, at dinner, his grandfather asked whether he had helped his teammate. "I think so," Carson said. "I'm not sure which part did it. The belief or the specifics." His grandfather passed him the potatoes and said, "Most things worth doing have more than one part," and let it go at that.

Sunday evening Kassidy sent the new video. He watched it in the study with the door open, the last light coming through the window and catching the dust over his grandmother's boxes. The middle minute held. At 0:47 she advanced instead of restating, and she looked up from the floor and straight into the lens. He typed, "That's the one," and pressed send.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
Adam had signed up for Playwriting because it met in the auditorium, and the auditorium had seats you could nap in during last period. This theory lasted four minutes into the first class, when Mr. Kobayashi announced that everyone would write a ten-minute play and stage it before winter break, using the stage, the lights, and whatever classmates they could bribe with vending machine snacks.

The assignment sheet said "a moment from your own life," which Adam read as an invitation to include everything. His summer had contained six locations, minimum. There was the lake where Nico had tried to teach him to skip stones and he had instead skipped his phone off a rock; there was the bus station; there was his grandmother's kitchen with the radio that only got one station; there was the hospital waiting room, which he had not told anyone about except Elena, and only then in a text so full of typos it had taken her an hour to decode.

He wrote all six locations into the first draft anyway. The play was called "August," and it was eleven pages, and by page three the stage directions read: "The lights change to indicate we are now at the lake. Then they change again to indicate the bus station."

Elena read it during lunch with the expression of a connoisseur examining a wine that had gone off. "Adam. My love. What is this."

"It's my summer."

"It's a travel brochure with feelings." She flipped pages. "Where do I even stand? I'm in the lake scene and the hospital scene and somehow also a corn maze that I don't remember happening."

"That was interpretive."

She put the pages down and looked at him, which was worse than the lambasting he'd been bracing for, because she said nothing at all. Then she said, "Kobayashi told us the first day. A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people." She tapped the stack. "You were napping."

"I was resting my eyes strategically."

"You drooled on the syllabus. It's laminated. There's a tide line."

He took the pages back and stared at them. Six locations meant the play was mostly him telling the audience where they were, like a tour guide with a grudge. The lake, the bus station, the kitchen, the waiting room: they weren't scenes, they were labels. Meanwhile the one thing that had actually mattered that summer, the thing he hadn't been able to say out loud in any of those places, was sitting in the middle of page four without a stage around it at all.

Rehearsal was Thursday after school. Nico had agreed to be in it under the impression that it involved a corn maze. "I'm here for the corn maze," he announced, arriving at the auditorium with a bag of gas station popcorn, as if to method-act his readiness. He climbed onto the stage, stood where Adam pointed, and delivered his first line with a lugubrious gravity that would have suited a funeral and did not suit "Do you think the bus is late or just slow."

"It's not the bus scene anymore," Adam said. "We cut the bus. And the corn maze. And, actually, five of the six places."

Nico sat down on the edge of the stage, dangling his legs into the orchestra pit's shadow, and processed this betrayal one kernel of popcorn at a time. "So what am I in?"

"One room. Two people. You're mostly playing my grandmother's radio."

"I could be the radio," Nico allowed, brightening. "I do static."

The new draft was one setting: the hospital waiting room, but staged as a kitchen, a radio on the counter, two chairs, a window that was really just the light booth with a gobo on it. He still wasn't sure that was honest. The true version of that summer had happened in six places, spread out and scattered, and compressing it into one room felt like a lie of a different kind, tidier than the truth. But when Elena ran lines with him under the work lights, something odd happened: with nothing to change and no tour to narrate, the two characters had nothing to do but talk, and what they said got closer to the thing he hadn't said all summer than anything in the eleven-page version had. The form wasn't shrinking the story. It was cornering it.

Mr. Kobayashi watched the run-through from the fourth row and took no notes, which everyone knew was either very good or very bad. At the end he said only, "Turn the radio off in the last minute. Let the room be quiet," and left, and Adam wrote that in the margin before he could forget it, because it was the only note and therefore the whole note.

The night of the winter showcase, Elena stood in the wings holding the flashlight they used as a lighting board, since the actual board had a policy of shutting off at random intervals. "Places," she whispered, and Nico raised one hand, wiggled his fingers, and began to hum, quietly, the static of a radio tuned to the only station it could get.

Adam stepped into the light, into the one room, and waited for the kitchen to become a waiting room, and waited, and it did.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
The hallway outside the gym smelled like floor wax and orchids, and Jayden stood in his gown with the yearbook under his arm, waiting for Mr. Castillo to come out of the faculty room. He had signed almost everyone's book already, sloppy loops of good luck and stay in touch, but Mr. Castillo's page was still blank, and it bothered him more than it should have. The plan was simple: get the signature, find Carolina and Ben in the band of chairs, graduate. The plan had already gone wrong once, because the advisory list he'd found while cleaning out his locker had reminded him of the kid he used to sit next to in ninth grade, the one who'd stopped coming sometime junior year, and Jayden had spent the last ten minutes wondering whether he should even be celebrating.

Carolina found him first, cap crooked, holding two programs she'd apparently decided to fan herself with. "They're seating us by last name," she said. "So I'm three rows behind you, which is basically a tragedy." Then she saw his face and lowered the programs. "What."

"Nothing. I was cleaning my locker and I found the freshman advisory list."

"Oh," she said, and the hallway noise went on around them, chairs scraping somewhere behind the gym doors, a teacher calling for the A through D row. "You counted."

"I counted." There had been twenty-six names on the list. He had counted the caps he expected to see across the stage, and the numbers didn't match, and the difference had a shape to it, a specific absence, like a tooth gone from a row.

Ben came over adjusting his tassel and heard the end of it. "Economics ruined you," he said. "You used to be normal. Senior year, Mr. Castillo's class, everything's a statistic. Remember when you made us listen to a whole explanation of stagflation at lunch? Prices going up and the economy going nowhere at once, and you thought it was fascinating, and I ate my fries."

"It was fascinating," Jayden said, but without force, because Ben had a point and they both knew it. He had spent the spring learning to see the world in aggregates, and now the aggregate had followed him into his own graduation, and it wouldn't let him just be happy.

Mr. Castillo came out of the faculty room carrying his own gown over one arm, and Jayden stepped forward and held out the yearbook, open to the page he'd been saving. "I wanted to ask you something first," Jayden said. "Something from class. The adjusted cohort graduation rate. The US average for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. Is that still about right?"

Mr. Castillo signed his name in a slow, deliberate hand before answering, which was typical, and Jayden waited while the hallway thinned behind them. "Roughly, yes," Mr. Castillo said. "Why tonight?"

"Because I found the advisory list, and I counted, and the missing ones aren't a rounding error to me. But the number is real too. I can't figure out which one I'm supposed to feel."

Mr. Castillo handed the book back. "Then don't figure it out tonight. Feel both and walk across the stage anyway." He moved off toward the gym, and Jayden watched him go, annoyed at the advice and already taking it.

They were called in alphabetical order, and Jayden's row advanced by degrees, the ceremony torpid in the way of all ceremonies, the principal's voice dragging between names like something too heavy to lift. From his seat he could see the families rising one by one in the bleachers, phones held up, and he thought of the kid from advisory, whose name he now made himself remember, DeShawn, no, only the allowed names, whose face he remembered even if the name had gone soft at the edges. Thirteen percent, he thought, on average, and some fraction of it standing in that kid's shoes, and no statistic anywhere that could tell him what had happened, or whether a phone call in October of junior year would have changed anything. He had not made the call. That was the part he kept circling back to, the fact that the aggregate was clean and his own conduct was not.

When his name was read, he crossed the stage, shook hands, received the case with the diploma inside it, and from the stage he could see over the whole gym: the caps, the parents, the exits at the far corners. Carolina, three rows back, was applauding with her programs. Ben had already shifted his tassel and was grinning up at whatever came next. Jayden held the diploma against his chest, and for a moment the two things he could not reconcile sat side by side, the whole row of them in white and green and the empty chairs that had once had names, and then he descended the stairs on the far side and joined the line of graduates filing out.

Later, in the parking lot, someone's older brother had set up a folding table with a sheet cake, and the class gathered around it in the long gold light. Carolina cut slices and passed them down the line, and when one slice fell apart in her hand she ate it herself and gave the next one away whole. Jayden stood at the end of the table with his cap under his arm, and Ben came over and put a flattened piece of cake on a napkin and said, "Okay, statistician. Say something dumb about the future."

"Thirteen percent of nothing," Jayden said. "Eighty-seven percent of us are standing right here, and I'm going to spend a while thinking about the rest."

"That's not dumb," Ben said. "But it's fine. Cake?" and held out the napkin, and Jayden took it, and ate it standing up, and watched the last buses pull out of the lot behind the school.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
story:
Mya stood in front of the Kahlo for eleven minutes before she wrote a single word, and in that time three separate people asked her to please step back from the rope. The assignment sheet in her pocket said "formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism," as though these were three tidy drawers she could open one at a time. The painting, a self-portrait ringed with green foliage, a red shawl, a hummingbird dead on a thorn necklace, refused to be tidy. Her friend Esteban had finished his notes in the gallery café twenty minutes ago and had come back to find her exactly where he had left her, arms crossed, pen uncapped and untouched.

"You look like you're mad at it," he said.

"I'm not mad at it. I'm mad at me." She held up her notebook, which contained one sentence: "The colours are intense." Esteban read it and made a sympathetic noise, the kind you make at a dying houseplant. "Mr. Ho is going to write 'so what' in the margin. He wrote it on my last essay four times. Once in the margin, once at the end, and once, I swear, in the middle of a word."

"That's because you equivocate," Esteban said. He had the frankness of someone who had already turned in his draft. "You write 'perhaps' and 'arguably' until the reader forgets what you're arguing. Just say the thing."

The thing, unfortunately, was the problem. Mya could feel the thing, physically, standing there. The red of the shawl and the green of the leaves seemed to push against each other, to hum at some frequency just below hearing, so that her eyes wouldn't rest anywhere. She had half a notion from a unit they had done in September, something about a colour wheel, but the memory came back to her the way a word comes back on the tip of your tongue, shapeless and irritating. She closed her eyes, which a passing guard noted with visible suspicion, and tried to picture the wheel her Grade Nine teacher had drawn on the whiteboard. Twelve slices like a boreal summer pie, she had thought at the time, because even the yellows had looked cold to her, like tundra lichen. Where had red sat? And green?

"It's opposite," she said suddenly, opening her eyes. "Red and green. They're opposite each other on the colour wheel. Opposite each other. They're called complementary colours."

"Congratulations," said Esteban. "Should I clap?"

"Esteban. If they sit side by side, they make each other look brighter. That's why the shawl is screaming at the leaves. That's why her face is the calmest thing in the whole frame, because everything around it is vibrating." She was writing now, fast, her handwriting collapsing into its emergency script. "It's not just intensity, it's placement. She put the two loudest colours next to each other on purpose, so that the middle, her own face, stays quiet. The composition does the same thing. Everything symmetric, the monkey on one shoulder, the cat on the other, the arch of leaves like a frame inside the frame. And then the hummingbird, dead, right at her throat, hanging off the thorns."

Esteban leaned in and considered the bird. "So what is the hummingbird." He said it in Mr. Ho's exact cadence, which was unkind and also, she had to admit, funny.

"That's the symbolism part and I don't know yet. Freedom that's dead. Or freedom that's heavy. Or it's a joke about hope, because hummingbirds were supposed to bring luck, and hers is hanging upside down." She looked at the bird a while longer. The thorns dug into the painted skin, a single drop of blood on the neck, and Mya thought about how you could read the whole painting as either suffering worn like jewellery, or jewellery sharpened into suffering, and how she could not decide, and how maybe Mr. Ho did not want her to decide. Maybe a real critique was allowed to hold two readings at once, as long as you didn't hide behind "perhaps."

"I'll write it like this," she said, mostly to herself, pen moving. "The complementary reds and greens amplify each other so that stillness only survives at the centre. The symmetry promises order. The dead hummingbird breaks the promise. I read it as grief, but I'm going to say plainly that the bird could also mean luck she doesn't trust, and that the painting holds both."

"That's still two things," Esteban said.

"It's two things held. That's different from not choosing. There's a difference between a dilettante who can't commit and someone who actually looked." She snapped the notebook shut, then opened it again, because she had just thought of a much better opening sentence than "The colours are intense" and did not want to lose it in the walk to the café. Behind her the red shawl kept shouting at the green leaves, quietly, forever, the way Kahlo had arranged for it to.

"Buy me a coffee and I'll let you read my intro," she said, and Esteban was already holding the door.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
story:
Charles had taped the graph to the refrigerator because it was the only vertical surface in the kitchen still bare, and because his grandmother, who was convalescing on the living room sofa after her hip surgery, would pass it every time she limped to the window for light. The graph showed carbon dioxide measured at a place called Mauna Loa, a jagged line rising through decades like a sawtooth staircase, and it was due to be explained, out loud and convincingly, by him, on Thursday morning in Ms. Santoso's class.

The presentation was the problem. He understood the pieces separately. He knew that sunlight came through the atmosphere and warmed the ground, and that the ground gave off heat of its own, and that certain gases absorbed that outgoing heat and sent part of it back down, so the planet stayed warmer than it otherwise would. He could recite that. But when Valerie had quizzed him after school, sitting on the wall outside the gym with her sneakers swinging, he had stumbled over the simplest question, which was why the line wiggled up and down every year while still climbing. "If it's cars and factories," she had said, "why does it drop at all?" He had said something about seasons, felt it come out vague, and watched her face do that thing where she decided not to press him.

His grandmother, whose name was the only one on the mailbox now since his grandfather's death in the winter, called him in from the hallway. She was propped on pillows with a blanket over her knees and a cup of tea going cold on the side table. "Charles," she said, "come tell me what that picture on the fridge means. Your mother says you have to talk about it."

He brought his notebook and sat on the arm of the sofa. He started where Ms. Santoso had started, with the atmosphere as a kind of blanket, but he saw her frown and stopped. "A blanket traps your heat because it stops the air moving," he said. "That's convection. This is different. It's radiation. The gases don't block the warm air, they absorb the heat rays themselves, the infrared, and re-emit them, and some of that goes back toward the ground."

"You lose me at infrared," she said, "but keep going anyway."

So he pointed at the graph, tracing the little teeth. "The planet breathes," he said, and as he said it he understood it for the first time, because he had spent the weekend reading about forests in the north. "In summer the plants pull carbon dioxide in, so the line dips. In winter, when the northern hemisphere goes dormant, it climbs back. That's the wiggle. But underneath the wiggle the whole thing rises, every single year, because we keep adding more than the plants and oceans can take back." She nodded slowly, and he felt the explanation settle into place in his own head, the way a shelf does when you finally get both brackets level.

The flash of memory came without warning: his grandfather's hardware store, the year it went under. Charles had been eleven, and had helped carry boxes of unsold inventory to the basement, breathing dust, while his grandfather climbed a ladder to take down the sign himself rather than pay anyone. Later his mother had used the word insolvency on the phone to her sister, quietly, in the hallway, and Charles had looked it up: not just being poor, but the specific condition of owing more than everything you had. He had thought of it all winter as a family word, a private catastrophe. Now, sitting beside his grandmother, he thought of the graph the same way, a ledger of something spent faster than it was paid back, and he almost said this out loud and didn't, because it sounded like something a person says to sound deep.

"What year is that?" his grandmother asked, tapping the paper with one finger. She had found the spot where the line crossed a printed mark, a horizontal rule someone had drawn at 400. "Where it goes through that line there. Was that recent?"

Charles leaned in. He had read it and reread it, and had gotten it wrong once already, telling Dave on the bus that it happened in 2015, and Dave, who had actually done the reading, correcting him without gloating. "May 9, 2013," Charles said now. "The daily average at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million that day. First time in the whole record."

"First time since they started measuring, or first time ever?"

He hesitated, because that was exactly the distinction he had fumbled with Dave. "First time in the record," he said. "That's what it says. The record. What came before the record, I don't know from that." His grandmother accepted this with a small sound, half approval, half disappointment, and he recognized the feeling himself: the honesty was worth something, but it wasn't the same as knowing.

That night Valerie called him, not about the presentation, about the argument she was having with Dave, who believed nothing individual people did mattered next to a hundred companies, and who said so at lunch with his arms crossed. Valerie believed the opposite, or wanted to. "You're the one with the graph," she said. "Tell me it means something if I ride my bike."

Charles sat on his bedroom floor with the phone on speaker and the graph flattened beside him under his desk lamp. He thought about the ledger, the breathing planet, the shelf with two brackets. "I don't think it's either of those by itself," he said. "The line rises because of big systems, so Dave's right that a bike won't bend it. But the systems run on demand and law, and demand and law are made of people, so you're right that it doesn't start without somebody. I'm going to say that on Thursday and see what happens." There was a silence on the line that he let sit, because he did not actually know if it was a good answer, and he was tired of covering not-knowing with confidence.

The vestigial radiator under his window, left over from the days before the house had central heat, ticked as it cooled. On Thursday morning he stood in front of Ms. Santoso's class with the graph projected behind him, took a breath, and touched the screen where the line crossed 400. "This day," he said, "May 9, 2013."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video had been shared four hundred thousand times by the time James saw it, and he had added his own thumb to the count before lunch without thinking. Now, in the computer lab, with rain making the tall windows look diaphanous and the radiators clanking like something being murdered, he opened it again. A flooded street, a car floating past a shop with a sign he couldn't read, a man's voice shouting in a language James didn't recognize. The caption said THIS IS HAPPENING RIGHT NOW IN EUROPE, and below it a chain of comments, furious and grieving and certain.

"You shared that too," said Alexane, two seats over, not looking up from her screen. She had a way of knowing what he'd done without being told, which he found flattering and also terrifying.

"I shared it first, actually." He turned his chair. "Leia forwarded it to me, but I was the one who sent it to the group chat. So if it's fake, that's on me."

Leia spun around from the front row, where she was supposed to be transcribing her chemistry notes from a photo of the whiteboard. "It's not fake. My cousin in Brussels says the weather's been insane there."

"Your cousin said that about a hailstorm in June," Alexane said. "That is not evidence."

James dragged the video into the image search bar, because that was the obvious move, the move that felt like competence. The engine refused it flatly, the little box going pink, the file type rejected like a student without a hall pass. He tried another engine with the same result, then a third, typing faster, as though speed could change what the software would accept.

"You can't put a video in," Leia said, drifting back to watch over his shoulder. She smelled of the cafeteria's orange juice, which she drank at all hours like a legal stimulant. "My brother told me. Fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead."

"Screenshots," James repeated. The obvious, once someone else said it, was humiliating. He scrubbed to the frame with the shop sign, paused, took a screenshot, and fed the still image into the search. The wheel turned. Behind him the lab printer groaned through someone's history essay with a throughput of roughly one page per geological era, and Ms. Horváth, who supervised the lab on Tuesdays, told it quietly to settle down.

The results came back. The same image, the same flooded street, the same floating car, dated three years earlier, on a news site, in a language that the browser offered to translate. Not Brussels. Not now. James sat very still, the way you do when a door you'd been leaning on opens.

"So it's old," Leia said. "That doesn't mean the flood wasn't real."

"No," James agreed. "It means the flood was real three years ago, somewhere else, and someone put a new caption on it and made four hundred thousand people feel something today that wasn't happening."

Alexane pulled her chair over. "Are you going to post the correction?"

He looked at the group chat, already scrolled far past his share, forty new messages about something else entirely. A correction would land in the void like a stone in a moving river. He could transcribe the links, write it out cleanly, tag everyone who'd commented, and maybe two of them would read it, and one of those two would say the news site was also lying, because that was always someone's next move. Or he could say nothing, which was what he'd done last autumn when a different video went around, a hospital one, and he'd privately suspected it and said nothing, and the not-saying had sat in him all year like a swallowed coin.

"There's a thing I didn't check in October," he said. "A clip from a hospital corridor. I had a feeling about it and I didn't even try. I just let the feeling be the whole decision."

"That's very dramatic," Alexane said. "It was a group chat."

"It was four hundred people."

"It's still a group chat," Leia said, but she said it gently, and she had pulled up the comment thread under the flood video and was reading it with her chin on her hand, her face doing the thing it did when she was changing her mind in real time and didn't want anyone to watch.

Ms. Horváth came down the aisle collecting the printed essays, paused at their screens, and raised an eyebrow at the flooded street, the floating car, the three-year-old date. "That was a bad week," she said, only that, and moved on.

James opened a new message. He typed, deleted, typed again. Behind him the printer produced another page, unhurried, certain of itself, and Leia leaned over and said, "Start with the screenshot. Show them the screenshot."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
William had until six o'clock, when Sofia came to pick up the painting, and by four he had managed only to ruin it.

The backyard table was littered with tubes whose names he had trusted for years, cadmium red, ultramarine, and now none of them seemed to agree with each other. He was trying to paint her a graduation gift, a view of the ravine behind the school where they had spent September afternoons skipping stones, and the colors kept fighting. The orange he mixed for the turning leaves sat on the canvas like an accusation. He scraped it off with a palette knife and the canvas beneath came up in a thin curl, which felt like a verdict on the whole enterprise.

Benson arrived through the side gate without knocking, the way he always did, carrying two cans of soda and a truculent expression that softened only slightly when he saw the canvas. "It looks like a traffic accident," he said, setting a can down on the table.

"Thank you for your support."

"I mean it nicely." Benson sat on the picnic bench and studied the mess. "Why don't you just do what you always do, green trees, blue sky, done?"

"Because that's not what the ravine looks like in October. It looks like everything is on fire and also drowning at the same time." William gestured at his reference photo, at the impossible overlap of amber and violet in the reflected light. "And every time I mix those two, I get mud."

Benson drank his soda and offered no wisdom, which was one of his better qualities. William wiped his hands and went inside for his phone, meaning to look up whether mud had a cure, and instead fell down a longer tunnel. Complementary colors, the search results said. Colors opposite each other on the wheel. He followed the phrase back to its source and stopped, soda-warm and suddenly attentive, at an image of an old engraving: a circle made of the colors of the spectrum, arranged like slices of a pie. The caption said Isaac Newton had done it in his 1704 book Opticks. Newton, the gravity man, the physicist. The color wheel that William's art teacher had taped above the classroom sink, the wheel every painter he knew treated like inherited law, had started with a physicist bending light through a prism.

He carried the phone back outside and set it on the table between the soda cans. "Newton invented the color wheel," he said.

"The fig bar guy?"

"The apple guy." William turned the phone toward him. "In Opticks, 1704. He took the colors of the spectrum and arranged them into a circle." He said it slowly, still testing it against everything he had assumed. "So the thing I've been treating like a rule from the art gods is basically a physicist's diagram."

Benson leaned in, squinting. "So when you put opposites together, is that physics or is that art?"

That was the question, William realized, and it sat on the table with the paint tubes. He had spent three years thinking of his physics class and his studio period as two locked rooms, one ruled by measurement and one by feeling, and had liked the separation because it excused him from being good at both. If Newton had drawn a circle to hold the spectrum together, maybe the wall between the rooms was thinner than he had believed. Or maybe Newton had simply made a convenient tool and artists had found their own uses for it, borrowed and transformed, and the circle meant different things to the two of them. William could not decide, and the deadline ticking toward six did not care.

He picked up the violet and the amber and laid them side by side without mixing, letting the border between them buzz the way the photo's border buzzed. Then he mixed a small amount of the two, deliberately, watching the mud arrive on the palette. But now the mud was information instead of failure. It was a boundary condition, a place where the two systems touched and gave ground. He painted the shadowed water with it and, against it, the unmixed colors burned brighter than they had all afternoon.

"Better," Benson admitted.

"It's not done." William checked the time. Five-fifteen. The ravine was emerging, but the painting had cost him the whole weekend he had promised to his father for clearing the garage, an encumbrance of a different kind that would meet him at dinner. And the colors still weren't the ravine, only an argument about it, a compromise between what light did and what he wanted.

At ten to six he set down the brush. Sofia's car pulled into the driveway and her footsteps came around the side of the house, and William stood in front of the canvas with his hands stained amber to the wrist, still unsure whether what he had made was a painting or a diagram.

She stopped at the gate and looked at it for a long moment. "It's the ravine," she said. "It's exactly the ravine."

William glanced at Benson, who raised his soda can slightly, and then he carried the painting, still tacky at the edges, toward the front of the house.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The last Sunday of September had a way of filling the house whether anyone planned it or not. John's father claimed the good chair by two o'clock, his mother set out the chips she always saved for occasions that weren't quite occasions, and this year Brittany and Marisa came over with a bag of licorice and their own opinions about the secondary. The neighbor, Ms. Villanueva, appeared at the door near kickoff holding a bowl of something with lime in it, and nobody had to ask her to stay.

John's little cousin, eight and eager, wedged himself into the corner of the couch with the solemnity of a judge taking his seat. On the screen the field stretched away under the lights, that impossible green, and when the offense broke the huddle the yellow line appeared across it, bright and certain as a painted stripe.

"Who paints that?" his cousin asked. "Like, before the play? A guy runs out with a roller?"

Marisa laughed into her licorice. Brittany said, "It's probably just, like, part of the field," and then, less certain, "isn't it?"

John had never thought about it. He was eighteen and leaving for college in a week, and all summer he had been trying to assemble himself into someone who knew things, who had a considered answer ready. He looked at the line. It sat over the grass, and when a receiver's foot crossed it, the line didn't smear or smudge the way paint should. It looked, he thought, less like matter and more like weather, something laid over the image rather than over the ground. The pelagic blue of the field seemed to slide beneath it untouched.

"I don't think it's real," John said slowly. "I mean, I don't think it's on the field at all. I think it's on the broadcast."

His cousin looked betrayed. "It's right there," he said, pointing with a whole arm, as though proximity were proof.

"Let me check," John said, and pulled out his phone. Marisa leaned over his shoulder, chewing. He typed carefully, half afraid the answer would be boring, that the line would turn out to be some dull hydraulic sprinkler thing. Instead the result surfaced clean and strange: the yellow first-down line was computer-drawn. It had first been broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.

"Sportvision," John read aloud. "That's the company that did it. First time was ESPN, September 27, 1998."

"Before I was born," his cousin said, hushed, as if John had produced a fossil.

"So it's fake?" Brittany asked.

"No," John said, and then stopped, because the word wasn't right and he wanted the right one. "It's real, it's just not painted. It's drawn on the picture, not the grass. Like, the players walk over it and it doesn't rub off because there's nothing there to rub." He hesitated, honest with himself about the edge of it. "I don't totally understand how they keep it under the players instead of over them. That part I'd be guessing at."

His cousin absorbed this with visible effort, chin on his knees. Down in the game a cornerback interposed himself between receiver and ball, and the whole room gasped at once, Ms. Villanueva loudest, her bowl trembling on her lap.

"Cowabunga," his cousin said then, and Brittany snorted. "That's so old."

"It's a colloquialism," Marisa said primly, which made it worse, and his cousin grinned as though being outdated were a title he had earned.

Later, after the game had gone final and the kitchen had emptied and refilled with the smell of his mother's chili, John's cousin tugged his sleeve near the counter. "Do you think the players can see it?"

John thought about it. Eighteen years old, a week from a dormitory, standing in the warm light of the kitchen with an eight-year-old waiting on his word. "No," he said. "I think it's just for us."

His cousin considered the yellow line that lived only in the television, visible to millions and to nobody on the field, and then asked if they could go outside and paint one anyway, in the driveway, with the old chalk.

"Get your shoes," John said.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
The textbook open on Hannah's bed was wrong about her, she had decided, because it claimed that anyone could learn binary search in an afternoon, and it was now nine in the evening and she still could not make the numbers behave in her head. She had a quiz on Monday in Mr. Nguyen's class, the kind where you had to trace the algorithm by hand and say why it worked, not just run it, and the difference between the two had begun to feel like the difference between swimming and explaining swimming. Downstairs her mother watched something with laugh track; upstairs, Hannah drew a list of numbers on graph paper and cut it in half with a pencil stroke, then cut the remaining half in half, and lost her place.

She texted Shayden first, because Shayden understood panic in a way Aaryan never would. "did you get the search stuff," she typed, and the reply came fast: "no. nguyen might as well be speaking icelandic." That made her feel less alone and no less stuck, which she was beginning to suspect was the entire function of friendship.

Aaryan answered an hour later, when she had given up on the graph paper and moved to the kitchen for cereal. "easy," he wrote. "want to race? i do linear, you do binary. million word list, one word to find." She typed that she didn't have a million words, and he sent her a link to a file he'd built, a plain text list, alphabetized, of a million words, real and invented and everything between. "pick a word," he said. "tell no one. i'll find mine, you find yours, count your comparisons."

She set the laptop on the kitchen counter and chose a word, quietly, so that even the room could not hear it: lantern. Then she thought about what she was actually supposed to do. A linear search meant starting at the top of the list and checking each word in order, which would work, eventually, the way walking everywhere would work. But the list was sorted, and there was something in the sorting she had not yet learned to use. She went to the middle of the file, looked at the word there, and saw instantly whether lantern came before or after it. After. So she threw away the whole first half. Middle of what remained. Before. She threw away another half, and another, and the list shrank under her hands like paper being folded.

She was counting, though she kept losing the number, and had to start over twice with her finger pressed to the screen, whispering aloud in the empty kitchen, which was the kind of thing she would deny later. When she finally landed on lantern, highlighted at line 403,887, she counted the checks she had made on her scrap paper. Twenty. Nineteen or twenty, depending on whether the first glance counted, but never more than twenty. Aaryan's word, it turned out, sat near the end of his alphabetical range, and he reported a number in the hundreds of thousands, and then a second message: "you cheated." "it's called binary search," she wrote back. "that's the whole point. it only works because the list is sorted." There was a long pause, then: "huh." Then, grudgingly: "rematch saturday."

She sat with her cereal going soggy and did the thing that had failed her all afternoon: she tried to say why. Not the steps, the reason the steps were allowed. Every time she cut the list in half, one comparison was buying her the right to ignore half a million words, and halving a million again and again, twenty times over, left you holding a single word. That was the whole argument, and it fit in one sentence, and she thought about how strange it was that a sentence could be true while taking an entire evening to become hers. She wrote it on the graph paper, under the failed drawings, as if filing it somewhere official.

Mr. Nguyen was outside when she took the recycling to the curb, though she hadn't known he lived on her street until that fall, when he'd waved once from his porch and she'd pretended not to see him. She almost went back inside. Instead she said, "I get it now. The search thing. I raced someone with a million words." He rocked on his heels and asked what she'd found. "Twenty comparisons. Twenty, and he had to check, like, half the list." She expected him to launch into one of his explanations, the kind that made Shayden disaffected and half the class doodle, but he only said, "Then you don't need Monday," and went inside, and she stood at the curb holding an empty bin, unsure whether she'd been complimented or dismissed.

Back upstairs she found Shayden's last message unanswered: "if you figure it out call me, i'm failing." She picked up the phone and then put it down, because here was the cost she hadn't planned for: whatever she now understood had come through Aaryan's file and her own hands, and it would not transfer through a summary, any more than the cereal box could taste of cereal. She would have to sit with Shayden, at a table, and make her cut the list herself and lose count twice and feel the fold happen under her own fingers. That was an hour she did not have this weekend, and she was going to give it anyway.

She opened her notebook to a blank page and began writing it out in order, the way Mr. Nguyen would want on Monday: linear search checks each item, binary search halves a sorted list, at most twenty comparisons for a million. Somewhere between the second and third line she heard her mother come upstairs and pause outside the door, and Hannah covered the page with her arm without thinking, the way she'd once covered a diary, and her mother said, "Still up?" and moved on to bed without waiting for the answer. Hannah lifted her arm and looked down at her own handwriting, which had stopped mid-word, and wrote the last line.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises refrigerating cooked food within two hours, or within one hour if the air temperature is above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Nicolas would tell anyone who asked that he already knew how to cook, and by the end of that week even he almost believed it. Ms. Clarke-Williams had assigned each student a plan: seven dinners, one shopping list, everything cooked on Sunday in batches and portioned for the days ahead. Nicolas chose chili, a tray of chicken thighs, rice, and a soup he described to his friends as having a long lineage, since his grandmother had supposedly made something like it, though he had never actually watched her cook anything.

The cooking itself went well enough, or so he reported. He browned the chicken without setting off the alarm, and when Julius leaned over his pot and said the chili smelled like a gym bag, Nicolas told him it was supposed to smell rustic. Johnny stood at the next station with a saucepan of instant noodles and said, "At least mine's honest." Ms. Clarke-Williams moved between them, tasting, adjusting, saying little, and Nicolas took her silence for approval, the way he took most silences.

The trouble came on Saturday. His class had a make-up session at the school's teaching kitchen, and afterwards Julius invited Nicolas and Johnny to his uncle's place out past the reservoir, where there was a fire pit and a dock and, that weekend, a heat wave. Julius's uncle worked a double shift and left them a cooler, a bag of charcoal, and the chili Nicolas had brought in a plastic container, which he assured them was famous in certain circles. He'd carried it out of the house at eleven in the morning and set it on the picnic table while they swam, because the cooler was full of soda and there was no room.

By three o'clock the dock boards were too hot to walk on barefoot, and the shade had shrunk to a handprint under the one scraggly oak. They ate the chili at lunch anyway, paper bowls balanced on knees, and there was plenty left. "Save the rest for dinner," Johnny said, already spooning the leftovers back into the container. Nicolas nodded. He was, by his own account, the most food-safety-conscious person he knew. He had once read an entire pamphlet in a dentist's waiting room.

The container sat on the picnic table through the afternoon. Nicolas noticed it, in the way you notice a door you keep meaning to lock, and each time he decided the heat would keep it fine, since heat preserved things, which was why his grandmother had canned tomatoes on the stove, if she had, which he now suspected she had not. When Julius brought it up at six, the sun still well above the treeline, Nicolas said, "It's fine. It's cooked. Cooking kills everything."

Johnny, who had said almost nothing all day, looked at the container for a long moment. "My mom does food safety training for a cafeteria company," he said. "I actually know this one." Nicolas waited, already assembling his rebuttal. "Cooked food has to go in the fridge within two hours," Johnny said. "And if it's over ninety degrees out, like today, it's one hour." He wiped his forehead with the back of his wrist. "It's been way past that."

The silence had a shape to it, and the shape was Nicolas being wrong in front of the two people least likely to forget it. "That can't be right," he said, but without conviction, and he took out his phone, stepped into the weak shade, and looked it up himself because he would not take anyone's word for anything, least of all Johnny's. The screen confirmed it, every number exactly as Johnny had said, and Nicolas read it twice as if the second reading might soften it. He thought about how the uncertainty had metastasized all afternoon, starting as a small doubt at eleven and spreading until it covered the whole container, the whole table, the whole day he had narrated to himself as a success.

"That's the whole pot," Julius said, peering in. "That's your whole week of dinners."

"I know what it is," Nicolas said. He carried the container to the fence line where the raccoons wouldn't get it, and stood there longer than dumping chili required. In Ms. Clarke-Williams's class he had been the one with the plan, the batch cooker, the boy with a lineage of soup, and now that version of himself felt like something he had invented on the walk to school and simply kept repeating until it stuck. He had learned to plan meals and shop for them and cook them ahead, and he had learned it well enough to be careless with it, which seemed to him a stranger thing than not knowing it at all. He wasn't sure yet which part he'd keep.

"Ramen when we get back?" Johnny said, from behind him. "I'll make the good kind."

"There's no good kind," Nicolas said. He came back and sat on the cooler, which was mostly empty now, and the three of them watched the sun go down over the reservoir in no particular hurry. "Next weekend," Nicolas said, "I'm bringing a cooler just for the food." Julius asked whether this was a promise or a plan, and Nicolas said, "Same thing," and Johnny, facetious to the last, held up a paper bowl and said, "Then I'm holding you to the lineage."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
story:
The thing nobody tells you about a restaurant kitchen is that it's mostly a classroom with better knives. I figured this out on my first Saturday at the community kitchen on Delmore Street, where Ms. Lindqvist ran a cooking program for teenagers who, according to my mother, needed to learn to feed themselves before college. My mother had many theories about my unreadiness, and I had allowed myself to be signed up mostly to prove her wrong, which I later realized was not the same as being motivated, though at the time the distinction felt unimportant.

"Carson, right?" Ms. Lindqvist said, handing me an apron stiff with starch. "You'll be with Jaeden and Marc-Olivier on soups. We're doing batch cooking today. Six quarts of minestrone, and it needs to be in the fridge by noon."

I said, "Got it," in the voice of a person who has watched a great deal of cooking television and considered this nearly equivalent to experience. In fairness to myself, I could dice an onion. In unfairness to myself, I believed this made me a cook.

Jaeden was already at the stove, and Marc-Olivier was arranging vegetables on the counter with the seriousness of a surgeon prepping instruments. They were both seniors from the school across the park, and they'd been coming since September, which gave them the patient manner of people waiting for the new guy to make a predictable mistake. I decided they were probably judging me, though it later occurred to me that they might simply have been chopping carrots. I have a habit of imputing judgment to people who are mostly just busy.

The soup came together faster than I expected. Too fast, actually. By eleven we had a vat of minestrone that smelled like something my grandmother would have approved of, and I felt a warm tide of accomplishment, which I mistook for competence. "Done," I announced, and reached for the lid.

"Where's it going?" Marc-Olivier asked.

"Fridge. Obviously."

He looked at the pot. It was deep, nearly a foot of soup, still steaming faintly in the center where I'd stirred it last. "You want to put that whole thing in the fridge?"

"It'll cool down," I said. "That's what fridges do."

Jaeden didn't argue, which I appreciated at the time and appreciate differently now. He just slid a stack of shallow plastic containers across the counter, the flat kind with the wide lids, and went back to his ladle. I stood there holding the pot handles and understood, slowly, the way you understand a joke at a party an hour after the party, that he was letting me arrive somewhere on my own. What I arrived at was a question: why would anyone bother with ten small containers when one large pot existed?

I asked it out loud. "Is this a dishes thing? Because I'll wash the pot either way."

"A pot that deep stays warm in the middle for hours," Marc-Olivier said, tapping the container tower. "Even in the fridge. Split it up, spread it out, it cools fast." He said it the way you'd say water runs downhill, like something he'd learned by ruining a batch once, and I filed it away with the small electric feeling I get when a system reveals its logic.

So we ladled. Ten shallow containers, lids cracked, staggered on the fridge shelves with air between them, and I confess I felt a certain pride in the apportionment, each container holding a single reasonable dinner, a week of lunches laid out in flat white rectangles. Ms. Lindqvist drifted past, opened the fridge, closed it, and said nothing, which from her was a standing ovation.

What I hadn't planned, and what nobody's cooking show had covered, was the rest of the week. On the drive home I did the arithmetic in my head, and it was here that my earlier confidence started to look like the problem rather than the solution. Batch cooking, it turned out, was not one skill but three braided together: planning a week of meals, shopping for exactly what they required, and then cooking in batches large enough to justify the effort but small enough to eat before boredom set in. I had done the third part only, and even that with the grace of a passenger who happens to be in the car when it arrives.

The following Saturday I brought a list. Marc-Olivier read it over and raised an eyebrow at the seven identical dinners of chicken and rice. "You're sanguine about your tolerance for repetition."

"I can eat anything," I said, and believed it in the way you believe you'd be brave in a fire.

By Wednesday I knew that I could not, in fact, eat the same chicken twice in a row without inventing grievances against it. I texted Jaeden, who replied that the point was a base, not a sentence: the chicken could become soup, or get thrown into the rice with the last of the salsa, or land on bread with whatever cheese had survived the week. This was a second way of thinking about the same containers, less like a plan and more like weather, and I sat on my kitchen floor with the fridge open and tried to hold both ideas at once. I am not sure I hold either one yet, honestly. The plan is tidy and usually wrong by Thursday; the improvising is alive and occasionally leaves me eating beans from a can at ten at night. Maybe the truth of feeding yourself sits somewhere between, and maybe it's different every week, which is either the disappointing part or the interesting one.

This Saturday we made soup again, and when the new kid reached for the pot lid, I slid the shallow containers down the counter without a word. He looked at me like I was inventing chores.

"Trust me," I said. "You'll want these."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The cuff hissed twice before it worked, and Dylan's father sat very still at the kitchen table with his sleeve rolled up, watching the numbers climb on the little screen the way he watched the doctor's face in March. Dylan had pulled the machine from the bathroom closet that morning and set it beside the cereal because Mr. Kamau, from next door, had said that morning readings meant something, and because Dylan wanted to stop guessing.

"Write it down," his father said, and Dylan copied 128 over 84 into the notebook he'd started, under yesterday's 126 over 82. The kitchen smelled of toast gone cold. He turned the notebook sideways and looked at the column of numbers like it might confess something.

Sara came over after practice, still in her track shorts, and sat on the counter with the last orange. "You're logging his blood pressure like a science fair project," she said. "Does he know?"

"He asked me to." That was mostly true. He had started it and his father had allowed it, which were not the same thing, and Dylan could feel the difference without being able to name it. "I don't actually know what the numbers mean, though. Like, is 128 bad? Is 126 bad? What's the line?"

"You could look it up."

"I looked it up. It's confusing because there's more than one guideline." He scrolled his phone and then read slowly, the way he read when he wanted to keep the words exact. "The 2017 one, from the cardiology and heart associations. Under that, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic." He said it twice, once to her and once to the notebook.

"Systolic's the top number," Sara said, pointing at his father's column with a segment of orange. "So even his good mornings are over the line."

"Under the line," Dylan said. "Over the number. It's under 120 that's normal, so he's above that." He caught himself enjoying the correction and let it go. "That's the thing, though. The number's clear and everything after it isn't."

Nixon arrived with his backpack still on, having heard from Sara that there were snacks, and he leaned over the notebook with the confidence of someone who had taken a health unit in grade nine. "My grandpa's on pills for this," he said. "Salt, basically. Too much salt and no walking. My mom talks about it constantly."

"See, that's what everybody says," Dylan said. "Salt, walking. But nobody says how much, or how fast, or whether it's the same for him. Everybody's got one sentence and they think the sentence is the whole thing." He had spent an interminable hour the night before on forums where people argued about potassium and sodium and cardio versus weights, and every answer had sounded certain and none of them had agreed.

Mr. Kamau knocked at the back door around then, returning the screwdriver Dylan's father had lent him, and stayed when he saw the machine on the table. He looked at the notebook, and at Dylan, and did not touch either. "You are the one doing this," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm trying to understand it," Dylan said. "My dad's numbers are above where normal is. Under the 2017 guideline, normal's below 120 over below 80, and he's not there. And I keep getting these one-line answers about diet and exercise like they're magic, and I don't want to hand him one line. I want to know what I actually know."

Mr. Kamau pulled out a chair and sat. "In my clinic," he said, and Dylan hadn't known he'd worked in one, "we had a saying. The guideline tells you where the door is. It does not tell you what is behind the door." He tapped the notebook once. "You have the door. Now walk through it slowly."

So they did, that evening, the four of them in the kitchen with the radio low. Sara made a chart on graph paper, sodium on one axis, walking on another, honest about the empty squares where they were guessing. Nixon suggested a month of walks with his grandfather's route along the canal, three evenings a week, Dylan's father welcome. Dylan wrote it all down, and at the bottom he wrote what he could defend and what he couldn't, in two columns, because pretending the two were one had started to feel like the actual danger.

His father came in at nine, read the notebook standing up, and was quiet long enough that Dylan could hear the fridge cycling.

"You'll measure me tomorrow morning," his father said. "Before coffee."

"Both numbers," Dylan said, and held out the cuff.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
Edouard's father adjusted the passenger mirror a third time, as though the whole lesson depended on it, then handed over the keys with the reluctance of a man surrendering a kidney. The car was an old grey sedan with a crack across the windshield and a smell of cold coffee, parked at the curb on Aldergrove Lane, where the maples had dropped their seeds and the street was quiet enough that a wrong turn would embarrass only the squirrels. Edouard slid behind the wheel, set his hands where the manual said, and started the engine.

"The following distance," his father said before Edouard had even put it in gear, "is three seconds. That's the National Safety Council, not my opinion. Count it out."

"Marcel says two," Edouard said. "He says three is for old people. He's been driving on his cousin's farm since he was twelve."

"Marcel can expiate his sins with the guardrail someday. Three seconds, and you add a second for every difficulty. Rain, heavy traffic, anything like that. Count from a fixed object."

Edouard eased out along the lane. The steering felt heavier than he expected, the way a door feels heavy in a dream, and the houses slid past with a slowness that still seemed too fast. He picked a driveway where the pavement changed shade and began counting under his breath when the car ahead passed it. One. Two. He was already through. He let off the gas until the count stretched, the sedan drifting back like a boat easing off a towline, and felt the strangeness of deliberately giving up ground in a race he hadn't known he was running.

They came to the four-way stop at the end of the lane, and Talon was there on the corner, standing at his mailbox with a stack of flyers for some food drive, watching Edouard stall the car twice and then creep through the intersection. Talon waved with both hands, mocking and glad at once, and shouted something Edouard couldn't hear over the engine. His father told him to check the mirror, and in the mirror Talon shrank to a small bright figure, still waving, and Edouard understood suddenly that from now on he would be the one inside the glass looking out at people who stayed where they were.

They turned onto the busier road, and the world changed. Traffic thickened, brake lights blooming ahead in a slow chain, and a drizzle started, dotting the windshield without quite justifying the wipers. His father said nothing, which was its own instruction. So that was it, Edouard thought: not one rule but arithmetic, the distance a living thing that grew with the road's difficulty. Three seconds became four, and then, when the rain thickened and a delivery truck cut in close, five, the gap widening in front of him like a held breath. Two seconds, Marcel's gospel, belonged to the farm, to gravel roads where the only thing to hit was a fence post. Here the road was a synecdoche for everything that could not be controlled, the small part standing in for the whole indifferent world, and Edouard adjusted to it without deciding that Marcel was wrong. Marcel's world was real too. He just didn't live in it.

They pulled into the car park of the strip mall to turn around, past the donation bin where the indigent man sometimes sat with his dog and a radio playing old salsa, though today the concrete was empty and shiny with rain. His father pointed at the bin. "When you have your licence, you can drop off those bags your mother's been tripping over." The ordinariness of it, the errand folded into the lesson, made Edouard's throat tighten. The licence was not escape, then. It was usefulness. Both at once, maybe, and he didn't have to choose today.

On the way back the rain eased and the traffic thinned, and his father told him to bring it back to three seconds and hold it steady. Edouard watched a hydrant go by and counted, one, two, three, the space ahead of him opening and holding like something he had built with his voice. He thought of telling Marcel about the extra seconds, the rain-second, the traffic-second, of arguing it out at lunch while Talon rolled his eyes, and he didn't know yet whether he would say it as a correction or as an offer. The street turned quiet again, the maples, the seeds on the pavement. Talon was still at his mailbox, damp now, pretending to rearrange the flyers.

Edouard brought the car to the curb in front of the house, not perfectly, a foot from the gutter, and set the brake. Talon ambled over and rapped a knuckle on the window. "So when are you driving us somewhere?"

Edouard rolled it down. "When I can count to five in the rain without my dad yelling."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
Emile had failed the cellular respiration quiz on Tuesday, and by Thursday he had memorized the whole pathway anyway, glycolysis to pyruvate to the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain, the way he memorized bus routes: usable, joyless, and gone within a month. He sat in the back of Ms. Le's classroom during lunch with the diagram flattened under his palm, tracing the arrows with a pencil so many times the paper had gone grey and soft at the folds. Allegra dropped into the seat across from him with her own sandwich and watched him work.

"You're doing the thing," she said. "The route-memorizing thing. You did it with the French verbs and then you couldn't order coffee in Montreal."

He demurred, but only verbally; his pencil kept moving. "The exam is in nine days."

Taylor came in behind her, shaking rain off his jacket, and put a printout on the table between them. It was a photograph, slightly pixelled, of a machine. Emile leaned over it. The thing in the picture looked like a mushroom made of engine parts, a stalk with a lopsided knob on top, and under the photo a caption read that this was ATP synthase, the enzyme that made most of the ATP in his cells, the enzyme whose steps he was supposed to trace. Below the caption, a second photograph showed the same enzyme with a curved arrow drawn around its head.

"It's from the science museum," Taylor said. "The one out by the river. They've got a model of it that actually spins. You crank a handle, protons flow through it, and the top part spins around, and every turn builds ATP. It's the size of a bicycle."

"Protons make it spin," Emile said slowly, and something in his chest rearranged itself, the way a room looks different after you move one chair. He had been thinking of respiration as a list. He had not once imagined that there was a motor in it, that somewhere in the membranes of his mitochondria there were literally spinning parts, thousands of them, turning in him at this moment, in the muscles of his hand holding the pencil.

"I've been tracing it like a map," he said. "Glucose to pyruvate, pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, on and on. But that's not what it is. It's a factory floor. There are machines."

Allegra tapped the photo. "So go see it."

The museum was open until six on Saturdays. Emile had planned to spend Saturday at his desk, because he was, by his own admission, something of an autodidact, happier teaching himself from textbooks than risking the embarrassment of being taught, and the desk was where autodidacts lived. He went anyway. Taylor came, and Allegra came, and they stood in the basement gallery in front of a model the size of a washing machine, its rotor made of yellow plastic, its proton channel a tube of clear acrylic. Taylor turned the crank. Protons, or bright blue balls standing in for protons, streamed down through the tube, and the yellow rotor spun, and on the other side, small white tokens dropped one by one into a tray. ATP, the label said. Emile turned the crank himself, slow, then fast, watching the spin and the tokens and the stream of blue, and he laughed once, alone, before he could stop it.

"Okay," Allegra said. "Tell me the whole thing. From the top."

He told her, there in the gallery, with his hand resting on the warm crank. Glucose gets broken open in the cytoplasm, a small profit of ATP up front. The fragments move into the mitochondria, into the matrix, and the Krebs cycle strips them for electrons. The electrons pass down the transport chain, and that chain pumps protons across the inner membrane, building up a crowd of them on one side. Then the protons flow back through ATP synthase, and the flow makes the enzyme's head spin, and the spin assembles ATP. "It's like the crank," he said. "Except nobody's cranking. The protons are the crank."

"What about the parts you still get wrong?" Taylor asked, because Taylor was like that.

"The chemiosmotic part. Why a gradient of protons counts as energy storage. I can recite it and I don't fully believe it yet." He was honest about this, and it cost him something to say in front of them, because for nine days he had been pretending the pathway was a thing he owned rather than a thing he was visiting.

Ms. Le was proctoring a make-up quiz on Monday, so Emile stayed after school on Wednesday to find her emptying the class aquarium, sleeves rolled, net in hand. He asked her about the gradient, and she asked him two questions back and then made him answer them himself, and at the end of ten minutes he understood it about eighty percent, which was, she said, more than most people ever get, and he believed her, mostly. On the exam the following Tuesday he traced the pathway cleanly, drew ATP synthase from memory with the curved arrow, and lost four points on a section about fermentation that he had decided, in his arrogance, no longer mattered.

He got the results on a Friday. Eighty-eight. Allegra, who had never once looked at a spinning model, got ninety-one. They stood at the bus stop in the late afternoon light, the diurnal world tilting toward winter, and she held her paper where he could see it.

"Next time," she said, "memorize the verbs."

"Next time," Emile said, "you're coming to the museum with me before the test, not after." He folded his exam along its old grey creases and put it in his back pocket, and the bus came up the wet road with its lights already on.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
Juliette had promised herself the meal would be perfect, and by perfect she meant that nobody would have to pretend. Her parents were coming home at seven, her mother from the clinic and her father from the airport, and she had the backyard to herself: the old grill, the folding table, her grandmother's recipe for lemon cake propped against a brick. She had watched her mother cook a hundred times and it always looked like weather, something that simply happened around her, so Juliette assumed it would happen around her too.

She zested one lemon, then realized the recipe needed three, and found only two in the bowl of fruit her father used for breakfast. The butter was still cold in the fridge. Halfway through creaming it with sugar, her phone buzzed on the table.

Adam had sent her a photo of his own kitchen disaster, a lumpy sauce, with the caption: "RIP." She sent back a picture of the cracked bowl, the half-zested lemon, the butter hard as a knob of chalk. Then she typed: do you have eggs? I need 4 and there are literally none here.

His reply came in three messages, one after another. "Go check before you start next time. My mom calls it mise en place. It's French, it means putting in place. Measure everything and prep everything before you cook." Then: "I have eggs but I'm at Nick's." Then: "Ask Morningstar. He bakes."

She sat on the back step with the phone in her lap, feeling the specific stupidity of someone who had believed enthusiasm was a substitute for procedure. She reread the messages. Mise en place. It was an anachronistic-sounding sort of discipline, like something from a nunnery, and it appealed to her and annoyed her at once, because it suggested that inspiration should wait outside until everything is chopped. She wasn't sure she agreed. Her mother improvised constantly, threw in cinnamon when the mood took her, and it worked. But her mother had thirty years of chops behind her, and Juliette had a cold stick of butter and no eggs.

Mr. Morningstar's yard was separated from theirs by a fence with a gap where a board had rotted. She found him deadheading his roses, and when she asked for eggs he didn't even ask why. "Four," he said. "Take six. They're from my sister's hens." He handed over the carton and then, as she turned to go, he said, "You're making the cake from the yellow card, aren't you. The one with the lemon." She stared at him. He shrugged. "Your grandmother and I traded recipes for twenty years. That one was mine before it was hers."

The twist landed strangely, the way a small fact can rearrange a whole childhood. She had always thought of the recipe as inherited, fixed, like her grandmother's handwriting. Now it turned out it had crossed a fence, the same fence she was climbing back over with the eggs. She set the six eggs on the folding table beside the two lemons, and then she did something she had never done before: she read the recipe all the way to the end, gathered every ingredient, measured the flour into a bowl, cracked nothing, melted nothing, until the table looked like evidence, arranged and waiting. Only then did she turn on the oven.

The cake went in. The chicken went on the grill. At ten minutes to seven her parents' car pulled into the driveway, and her mother came through the gate first, still in her scrubs, and stopped when she saw the table. "You did all this?" Her father stood behind her holding an airport bag and a bakery box with a ribbon on it, which he set down slowly, the way you set down something that has become unnecessary. Inside was a cake he had bought in the terminal because he hadn't trusted her to manage one.

Juliette took the lemon cake out of the oven, set it on the rack to cool, and looked at the two of them, the bought cake and the made one, and felt something in her that had been bleeding all afternoon quietly cauterize. She thought of Adam's messages again, the French words on her screen, and understood them differently now. Mise en place was not only about eggs. It was about deciding, before the heat started, what you were willing to lose. Though she could not have said whether her parents' marriage was a lemon cake or a bakery box, and she refused to hold a plebiscite in her own head about it, counting votes that were not hers to cast.
