Her mother cut a slice of the terminal cake anyway, out of kindness or exhaustion or something older, and said it was delicious. Juliette watched her take a second bite, and then her father reached over and, without a word, slid his fork onto the plate with the lemon cake and tried that one too.

"You used the yellow card," he said, chewing slowly. "It's better than I remember."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
I am not, as a rule, someone who lies to people I love. That is what I told myself all through the spring, and I believed it, the way you believe a song lyric you have sung too many times to hear anymore. The truth is smaller and worse: I told Layla her handoff was fine. It was not fine. She opened early on the second exchange at regionals, we went outside the zone, and the relay was disqualified, and afterward I put my arm around her in the parking lot and said the official was blind, that everyone saw she'd done everything right. Quinn stood a few feet away and said nothing at all, which I let count as agreement.

Layla turned eighteen in June, and her party was in Ms. Marino's backyard, because Ms. Marino had the pool and the long wooden fence and no opinions about how many paper lanterns were too many. I arrived late with a wrapped copy of a novel I hadn't read, and I found Layla by the drink table in her paper crown, and she said, "Next year, right? We go again," and I said, "Definitely," and the word sat in my mouth like a coin.

Quinn was by the fence, being Quinn, which is to say laconic in a way that reads as wisdom until you need an actual sentence out of him. He'd been my witness all season. He'd watched the same sloppy exchanges I had, the opened-early habit, the tensed shoulders on the curve, and he'd kept his mouth shut every single time because Layla cried easily and he hated making girls cry, and I hated it too, which was our whole philosophy, thinly disguised as kindness.

It was Ms. Marino's nephew, some college kid drifting between the pool and the table of chips, who ruined my comfort. He was telling someone about his summer internship, and I caught only a fragment, half a beer into the story he was telling a girl in a yellow dress. "My manager made us read this book," he said. "Radical Candor. 2017. Kim Scott. Her whole argument is that good feedback means caring personally about someone and challenging them directly. Both. At the same time."

I stood there with my cup sweating against my palm and felt the coin dissolve. Because I had been caring personally for a year. I had cared so personally that Layla never once heard the one sentence that might have fixed the handoff, and the team had paid for my tenderness with a season. Quinn, I realized, was not kind; he was absent. And I was not honest; I was comfortable. These were not the same things, though I had spent months treating them as if they were.

The problem, as I worked it out under the lanterns, was that neither of us knew what to do with the middle. Cruelty I understood. Silence I understood. What I did not understand was how to look at someone I loved and say the true thing with the specific detail attached, without padding it into mush. I didn't even know if Layla would want that. Maybe she'd rather have the amnesty I'd been granting her all year, the blanket pardon that lets everyone swim in the shallow end forever. That was the part I couldn't resolve, standing there, and I want to be honest: it stayed unresolved. I decided to act anyway.

I found her at the edge of the pool, feet in the water, crown wilting. I sat down and let the silence go on slightly too long, which is apparently my signature move.

"I lied to you," I said. "After regionals. The handoff wasn't fine. You've been opening early on the second exchange all season, and I saw it, and I never said anything because I didn't want to be the one who made you feel bad, and that was about me, not you." She didn't look at me. The water moved her feet in small circles. "You're faster than anyone in the county in the last hundred," I said, "and I want you on my relay next year, and I want us to actually get to states. So that's it. That's the whole thing."

Layla was quiet for long enough that I could hear the nephew laughing at something on the far side of the yard. Then she said, "Quinn said something to me Tuesday, actually. Almost the same thing. Two words, though. 'Your start.'" She pushed her hair off her forehead. "You two coordinate your honesty?"

"Heard it somewhere," I said.

She pulled her feet out of the water and looked at them, at the wrinkled pads of the toes, like she was checking them for damage. Then she said, "Say the early part again. The second exchange. What exactly do I do?"

I opened my mouth and the lantern light caught in the water and I began, carefully, with the curve.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
The keys felt heavier than they looked. Brayden turned them in the ignition of his grandfather's old sedan while Ms. Nasser settled into the passenger seat with her clipboard, and behind them, in the school parking lot, Amos leaned against the fence with his bike, waiting his turn.

"You're going to do fine," Ms. Nasser said. "Mirror, seat, and then out the gravel road to the county route. Quiet this time of morning."

Grandpa had driven him out to that same route last weekend, before his knees got bad, and had spent the whole trip talking. Ease up on the brake going downhill, he'd said. If anything ever runs out in front of you, pump the brakes, don't just stand on them. Brayden had nodded the way he nodded at grandpa's stories about milking cows by hand, half listening, filing it away.

Amos had a different file going. He'd come over Thursday with his learner's permit spread on the kitchen table and the owner's manual from his mom's car open beside it, because Amos read manuals the way other people read team standings. "This car's got anti-lock brakes," he'd announced, chewing a granola bar. "So if it's an emergency, you press the pedal firmly and just hold it. You don't pump. And you can still steer the whole time." He'd tapped the page like it was a verdict. Amos liked verdicts. He wanted to dichotomize everything into right advice and wrong advice, safe drivers and doomed ones, and he'd already held a private plebiscite on the matter and declared grandpa's method obsolescent.

"All right," Ms. Nasser said now, and Brayden let off the parking brake, checked his mirror twice because he was nervous and once more because twice hadn't felt like enough, and rolled out of the lot.

The gravel road was easy, long and straight, dust rising behind them like a shy tail. The county route was harder. It narrowed where the ditches deepened, and the November fields lay stripped and gray on either side, fence posts ticking past at a speed that felt indecent for something Brayden himself was producing. His hands were at ten and two exactly the way the pamphlet said, and they ached from it.

"Relax your thumbs," Ms. Nasser said. "You're not strangling it. You're holding it." He loosened his grip and the car seemed to breathe with him. She was good like that, noticing the small things, and when a truck ground past them the other way she said, "Well held," which made him feel seven feet tall for about a quarter mile.

He was beginning to enjoy it. That was the mistake, or maybe not a mistake, just the thing about driving: it forgave you for exactly as long as it felt like. Coming around the bend by the Hendersons' old barn, three deer came off the field and two crossed and one stopped, dead center in his lane, staring at him with a wet black eye, and everything in Brayden went bright and empty at once.

His foot did what grandpa had drilled into the family for fifty years. It lifted. It started to pump. And the pedal went strange under him, hard and gritty and buzzing, and the car was not slowing the way pumping was supposed to make a car slow, and the deer was still there, closer now, close enough that he could see the twitch of its ear. Then Amos's voice arrived in his memory, unhurried, mouth full of granola bar: press firmly and just hold it. You can still steer the whole time. Brayden pressed down hard and held it, the pedal buzzed against his foot like something alive, and he steered, the wheel answering him, the car tracking left into the empty lane while the deer broke right, and they passed each other with the whole width of the road between them and not one sound but the engine and his own breathing.

He pulled onto the shoulder, put it in park, and sat with his hands still on the wheel. Ms. Nasser let the silence run for a while, which he would be grateful to her for later.

"Anti-lock," he finally said. "It does that. The buzzing."

"It does that," she agreed. "You held it and you steered. That was the right thing." She wrote something on her clipboard, then looked up at the fields. "You all right?"

"Yeah." He wasn't sure that was true, but he also wasn't sure it was false, and both of those could be the case at once, he was discovering. He checked the mirror, signalled, and pulled back onto the road.

That night he called grandpa, not to correct him, because he wasn't going to correct his grandfather on the phone about fifty years of ice and gravel roads driven without a single deer in his lap, but just to tell him the story. "Buzzed like a hive," Brayden said. "The pedal, when I stood on it."

"Huh," grandpa said. "Ours never did that."

"They make them different now," Brayden said. "You press and hold, and you can still steer."

There was a pause long enough that he could hear the television going in the background, and then grandpa said, "Well. Keep that in the file, then."

"Which file?"

"The one your friend keeps," grandpa said, and Brayden laughed so hard he had to sit down on the stairs.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
Alexander had missed the Tuesday lab because of a dentist appointment, and by Thursday he understood that this had been a mistake of strategic proportions. Mr. Campbell's quiz on equilibrium sat on his desk, five questions, the last of which concerned a reaction in a sealed flask being heated and then left to settle. Alexander read it twice, then a third time, while across the room Hugo was already on question five, pen moving with the serene confidence of a boy who had copied someone's notes.

The problem gave an equilibrium constant K at 25 degrees and asked for the new equilibrium composition after heating to 60. Alexander did what felt reasonable: he carried the old K forward, set up his ICE table, and solved. The numbers came out clean, which he took as a good sign, though later he would learn that clean numbers in chemistry are rarely a good sign and usually a warning. He underlined his answer, added a small flourish, and handed the paper in four minutes early, which preempted any second thoughts.

Mr. Campbell returned the quizzes on Monday with the air of a man delivering difficult news gently. Alexander had a 62. Questions one through four wore red checkmarks; the last one wore a circle so large it enclosed his entire solution like a fence around a crime scene. Beside it, in tidy handwriting: see me.

He stayed after the bell, and found Cian already at the front desk, holding his own quiz. Cian had the same circle, the same fence. "I got the same answer as you," Cian said, as Alexander approached. "Exactly the same. That's how I knew something was wrong."

"Cheating off me would have been smarter," Alexander said. "At least then only one of us would be wrong."

Mr. Campbell, who had been watering the plants on the windowsill as though this had nothing to do with him, said, "Gentlemen, here is all I will tell you. Go back to the notes from Tuesday, the day you both squandered. Everything you need is on the handout." He set down the watering can. "And Alexander, your flourishes are lovely, but they cannot protect a wrong number."

The Tuesday handout was still in the tray by the door, that graveyard of papers for the absent and the disorganized. Alexander took two copies and he and Cian sat on the bleachers behind the gym, where the afternoon light came through the fence in stripes and the smell of the riparian trail behind the school drifted up whenever the wind turned. Cian read aloud, because Cian was an unapologetic raconteur even about worksheets, giving the sentences dramatic pauses they did not deserve.

"Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium," Cian read, "a change in concentration, a change in pressure, and the addition of a catalyst do not change the value of K." He looked up. "But temperature."

"Let me see it," Alexander said, and took the paper. There it was, the sentence, sitting quietly between a paragraph about pressure and a diagram of a flask. Of the common disturbances, only a change in temperature changes the equilibrium constant K. He read it aloud, slowly, and then sat back against the cold metal of the bleachers. "So on my quiz, I used the old K. But I heated it. I heated it and then used the old K."

"And I copied your setup," Cian said, "so we heated it and used the old K together. Like a team."

Alexander laughed, then stopped laughing, because the shape of it was opening up in his mind the way a diagram does when you finally see it in three dimensions. All term he had been thinking of K as a property of the reaction, fixed, like its color or its smell, something the reaction carried with it wherever it went. But it wasn't like that at all. It was a property of the reaction at a temperature. Heat it and you were not nudging the same equilibrium; you had a different one, with a different constant, and every answer downstream depended on knowing which you held.

"I want to say I understand it completely," he said. "I don't, yet. I understand that I was wrong, and I understand what the sheet says. Why temperature and not the others, I can't tell you."

"Mr. Campbell probably won't either," Cian said. "He'll make us figure it out with a flask and a thermometer and our own suffering."

That was more or less what happened. On Wednesday Mr. Campbell gave them each a fresh copy of the quiz question and a data table of K values at several temperatures, and said nothing except, "Check your answer against the table, then tell me what you did differently." Alexander worked through it with the corrected constant, watching the equilibrium shift the way the notes had promised, favoring the other side now, and when he finished he found Cian waiting for him at the bench with his own paper turned face down.

"Well?" Cian said.

"Show me yours first," Alexander said, and Cian flipped it over, and they leaned in over the numbers, heads almost touching, hunting for the difference.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
story:
The seminar room had been a greenhouse once, and the college had never quite decided what to do with that, so nineteen students sat in a horseshoe of tables under fogged south windows while Mr. He wrote a single question on the board: Should the county close the montane trails in the Nash drainage to protect the caribou herd? Julia copied it into her notebook, then drew a box around it, the way she did with things she did not yet trust herself to answer.

Levi sat across the horseshoe with his laptop open and his posture already arranged for victory. He had beaten her in the final round of the provincial debate tournament in the spring, on a resolution about toll roads, and he had been generous about it in a way that stung longer than gloating would have. Today he had requested the pro side, the closing side, and Mr. He had granted it, which meant Julia would speak first, which meant she could not simply answer him; she would have to think in front of everyone and let him think after.

She spoke from notes rather than a script. The county's own count put the herd at forty-one animals, down from sixty-three in the decade her family had kept the trailhead cabin, and the cows calved in the high basins the trails crossed. But the same report, three pages later, admitted that the count was taken in a single late-winter flight, in weather that had grounded the survey for two days. She said, "So if the number is wrong, everything built on it is wrong too, and I don't know which way it's wrong." Her voice caught once on the last clause. She sat down with her ears warm.

Levi stood. He had built something clean, she could see it even before he said it: the county must act where a population is in decline; the herd is in decline; therefore the county must act. He dressed the premises in survey numbers and a line about precautionary management, and it sounded like a wall. Across from her, Linkin was mouthing something, and she realized he was silently working through the shapes of the words, the way he did when he wasn't tracking meaning but phonetics, his other class; he could take an argument apart by ear the way he took a vowel apart, and he raised two fingers at her, quietly, like a man counting something he would not name.

Mr. He opened the floor. Someone from the far table asked about enforcement costs. Someone else asked whether hikers actually disturbed calving. Julia wrote nothing for a full minute. She drew the arrow of Levi's argument in her margin, premise to premise to conclusion, and tested each joint the way her father tested fence wire, pushing to see where it gave. The shape held. If the premises were true, the conclusion followed without a seam. She pushed on the second premise instead, the decline itself, and remembered the two grounded days, the single flight, her own October when she had counted eleven cows on the ridge where the survey later recorded four.

When Mr. He called the second round, she asked to speak before Levi could close. "Your argument is valid," she said, and watched him register that she was granting him something. "If those premises are true, the conclusion has to be true; I can't get out of it, and I'm not trying to. But a deductive argument is called sound only when it's valid and all of its premises are actually true." She kept her eyes on her notebook for that sentence, then lifted them. "The flight count is one premise, and I think it's false, or at least I think nobody knows. So the argument isn't sound, even though it's perfectly valid." She could feel the distinction landing unevenly around the horseshoe, settling with some students and sliding off others, and she let it.

Levi did not concede; that was not his way, and she would have been disappointed if it were. He argued that uncertainty cut his way, that precaution covered a shaky count as well as a solid one, and Julia felt the pull of it, because she had felt the same pull on the drive to the cabin each November, seeing fewer animals, wanting the trails closed on instinct before she wanted them closed on evidence. She stood once more and said, "Maybe precaution follows from uncertainty, but that's a different argument, and you'd have to build it from different premises. I might even accept it. But it isn't the one you gave us, and I don't want to accept the one you gave us by mistake."

Mr. He let the silence sit for a moment, then said the bell would end them whether they were finished or not, which was the closest he came to philosophy. Linkin passed her a torn sheet on his way out: a rough drawing of a bridge with one plank inked in red, and beneath it, "two fingers = the weak plank." She found Levi in the corridor by the water fountain, packing his laptop with the strap of his bag clamped in his teeth, and she waited until he had freed it. "Rematch on the precaution version," he said. "I'll have it built by Friday." She told him she'd want to see his premises before she saw anything else, and he laughed, short, and said, "That's the whole trouble with you." Down the corridor the linguistics lab was closing, a student clipping a sign to the door, and Julia folded Linkin's drawing along the bridge's spine and put it in her pocket.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
The summer before Kevin left for college, he played midfield for a team that practiced in Mr. Baptiste's backyard, because Mr. Baptiste had the only lot on the street long enough to run full sprints on, and because he had marked it with chalk lines every ten yards and let them use it in exchange for hauling his recycling to the curb. Kevin was good enough to start and not good enough to be noticed, which was a kind of freedom until it wasn't. In drills he ran hard when the coach watched and somewhere near that otherwise, and so did everyone, and nobody said anything about it, because saying something would have meant admitting they all knew.

The team lost four of its first five games, all in the second half, all on goals that came after their legs should have gone. The coach kept saying "we need more from everybody," which meant nothing and so was easy to ignore. Mattias, who played keeper and read everything, said the problem had a shape to it, though he couldn't name it yet. Alexi said the problem was that they were bad, which had the advantage of being unfalsifiable.

What changed the season happened at a practice in July. Mattias showed up with a stopwatch and a clipboard, both borrowed from his older brother, and announced that he was timing everyone's sprints, by name, every session, and posting the times in the group chat that night. Kevin's first reaction was indignation, which he kept to himself, and his second was the uncomfortable recognition that the indignation had arrived before any thought about fairness had. He simply did not want his number next to his name where the others could see it.

The first timed session was ugly. Kevin ran himself into the fence at the far end of Mr. Baptiste's yard, breathing like a landed fish, and his time was still slower than Alexi's, which stung in a way losing as a group never had. But by the end of that week something had shifted that he could see in the others before he could see it in himself. Nobody jogged through the recovery runs. Nobody hid at the back of lines. In the sixth game of the season they scored twice in the final twenty minutes and won, and Kevin, who had assisted on the second goal, understood that he had spent most of the season giving less than he had, not from laziness exactly, but because the group had made his less invisible.

Mattias finally found the word for it in a psych textbook his brother had left behind. "It's called social loafing," he said, tossing the book onto the grass between them. "The drop in effort people make in groups. It shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified." Kevin read the passage twice while Alexi peered over his shoulder. It was strange to see a thing you had done described so flatly, like finding your own handwriting in someone else's diary.

The costs arrived on schedule. Once the numbers were public, effort became partly a performance for the clipboard, and Kevin caught himself, more than once, angling his sprints so Mattias could see his face strain. Alexi, whose times stayed stubbornly mediocre no matter how hard he worked, started skipping practices, first one, then three in a row, a slow attrition that Kevin watched the way you watch weather coming. When he finally said something, it came out wrong, something about how Alexi owed it to the team, and Alexi looked at him for a long moment and said, "When it was just the team, nobody kept score on me."

That was the twist Kevin had not prepared for: the same clipboard that had pulled the group up had singled his friend out and set him apart. He sat on the porch steps at Mr. Baptiste's that evening after the others left, and Mr. Baptiste came out with two glasses of something cold and said nothing, which was his particular gift. Kevin turned the thing over without settling it. He believed in the times; he had seen them work, had felt himself work. He also believed Alexi, that a number beside your name could become a small cage. Both things were true and they did not lie down next to each other.

He tried to internalize the lesson the way you internalize a skill, through repetition, and found it would not cooperate, because it kept producing two lessons instead of one. Before the next practice he asked Mattias to keep timing the sprints but stop posting them in the chat, and Mattias frowned and said the whole point was that people could see, and Kevin said maybe the seeing could be smaller, just between the runner and the watch. They compromised on a folded piece of paper handed to each player privately, times written by hand, which was slower and somehow heavier than a group chat and which Alexi came back for.

They won the last three games of the season. On the final evening, after the others had gone, Kevin stayed to collect the cones and found Mr. Baptiste re-chalking the faded lines at the ten-yard marks, moving down the grass on his knees, careful as a man restoring something old. Kevin watched him finish the last mark and stand, brushing chalk from his hands into the twilight. "You'll want these next summer," Mr. Baptiste said, "or whoever comes after you will." Kevin looked down the whole measured length of the yard and said, "I'll leave the stopwatch in your mailbox, then. Where they can find it."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: Bigger samples help less than people expect: doubling a random sample from 1,000 to 2,000 people shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point.
story:
The phone bank had colonized Violet's living room by seven o'clock: three folding tables, a borrowed kettle, Jaydon's laptop balanced on a stack of her mother's old atlases. On the wall, because Jaydon had insisted, hung a hand-lettered sign reading VIOLET FOR STUDENT TRUSTEE, which was technically true, since she was running, and also absurd, since the election was five weeks away and she was eleven points behind.

"Eleven points," Mario said, spooning sugar into his third coffee. He said it the way a doctor says a number on a chart. "That's from the school paper's poll."

"Nine hundred and forty people answered," Violet said. "That's a lot."

"Margin of error was plus or minus three," Jaydon said from behind the laptop, where he was building the call list with the grim efficiency of someone who had discovered spreadsheets eight days ago. "So it could be eight, could be fourteen. Still behind."

Ms. Baptiste, who lived one floor down and had come up because she could smell the coffee through the vents, settled into the armchair with her knitting. She had voted in every school board election since 1987 and considered Violet's campaign the most entertaining thing to happen in the building all year. "Three points," she said mildly. "That seems very precise for nine hundred people."

Violet had assumed the same thing until Tuesday, when she'd gone to Ms. Baptiste's apartment to return a casserole dish and gotten a half-hour lecture on polls instead of the dish. Ms. Baptiste had worked thirty years for the provincial statistics office, and she kept saying the same pithy thing over the clack of her needles: "Everyone believes a bigger sample fixes everything. It doesn't fix as much as you want."

That had bothered Violet all week, the way a word misheard in a song bothers you. She'd assumed the world divided neatly into polls that were accurate and polls that weren't, and that accuracy was something you bought with volume, the way you bought coffee. She'd even built her whole strategy on it: more calls, more answers, more certainty.

She stood now in the middle of her own living room, holding the sign-in sheet, and made herself say it out loud. "Jaydon. If we double the calls, what happens to the margin of error?"

"Cut it in half," he said, not looking up. "Obviously. A thousand to two thousand, three points becomes one and a half."

"That's what I thought." She turned toward the armchair. "Ms. Baptiste. Tuesday you said something about doubling."

The needles paused. "I said doubling a random sample from one thousand to two thousand shrinks the margin of error by only about one percentage point." She resumed knitting, unbothered, as if she were reporting the weather. "Three points to about two. All that dialing, for one point."

The kettle began its low whine. Mario set down his mug. "That can't be right," he said. "One point. We call a thousand extra people for one point?"

"That's what doubling buys you," Ms. Baptiste said. "About one percentage point. A thousand more interviews for one point less wobble."

Jaydon finally looked up from the laptop. He was quiet for a moment, and Violet watched him arrive where she had arrived on Tuesday night, on the bus, staring at the window grime. The satisfaction of a plan, whole and simple, being quietly disassembled. All evening he had been subsumed in the fantasy of two thousand calls: the phone list as reparation for every lazy thing he'd ever done in a group project, the spreadsheet as proof of seriousness. Now the spreadsheet was still a spreadsheet, and the arithmetic underneath it had turned traitor.

"So my whole doubling plan," he said slowly, "buys us one point. We're still ten behind."

"Eleven," Mario said. "Plus or minus."

"Plus or minus more than we can afford to fix by dialing."

The kettle clicked off. Nobody moved to make the coffee. Violet sat down on the arm of the couch, the sign-in sheet soft in her hands, and thought about what Ms. Baptiste had said next on Tuesday, which was that a poll was a snapshot taken through a slightly dirty lens, and that people kept polishing the lens when what they needed was a different window. Violet hadn't fully understood it then. She thought she might now, or at least the part that mattered: the calls were still worth making, because every answer was a person who'd heard her name, but they weren't going to make the numbers confess anything they didn't already know.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," she said. "The poll says eleven. But eleven is a range, and ranges hide things. We could be at eight. Eight is closable. But I can't know that, and I can't get there by calling more people, so maybe the calls aren't about the poll at all. Maybe they're just the part where people hear from us."

"That is the least cynical thing you've ever said," Mario said. "I liked you better at eleven points down and furious."

"I'm still furious. I've just relocated the fury."

Ms. Baptiste laughed, a small dry sound into her wool. "That's politics, dear."

Jaydon turned the laptop around so they could all see the call list, four hundred names glowing in the lamplight, the living room suddenly small around it and smelling of coffee and radiator dust. "So we do the four hundred," he said. "Not two thousand. And you talk, and I dial, and we stop pretending the math is going to save us."

Violet picked up the first phone.

"Dial," she said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
The house had no furniture in it yet, only echoes and the smell of fresh paint, and Payton stood in the middle of the living room holding her phone against her ear while Ariel talked fast, the way she did when she was trying not to cry. "You'll forget us," Ariel said. "You'll get there and in two weeks it'll be like we never existed." Payton looked down at the bare floorboards, at the pale rectangles on the walls where the previous family's pictures had hung. "That's not how it works," she said. "I'm literally the one moving. I'm the one who has to start over."

She had read something online back in the spring, when the move was still rumor, a study by a researcher named Jeffrey Hall, and it had stuck with her the way certain facts do, lodging under the skin. Moving from casual friend to friend took about ninety hours together. Ninety hours. She'd done the math on the drive here, counting backward through four years of lunch periods and Saturday mornings and the summer they'd all worked at the pool, and she and Ariel were so far past ninety hours it was almost funny. The new people would be starting from zero.

The problem was that zero was zero. She told Jerome that on Tuesday, sitting on the tailgate of his truck in her driveway while the movers carried boxes past them into the empty rooms. "I did the math again," she said. "Ninety hours. That's like, if I see someone three hours a week, every week, it takes most of a school year." Jerome peeled the label off his water bottle in one long strip. "So start," he said. "You're good at starting things. You started the recycling thing at school and now there's a bin in every hallway." She laughed, but the laugh came out thinner than she meant. "That was bins," she said. "This is people."

She found the flyer on the community board at the grocery store, the one by the registers where the cashier was too busy to notice her standing there for ten minutes. River Cleanup Club, Thursdays, meet at the boat ramp. She didn't care much about the river, honestly, though the word riparian, printed on the flyer in a font that suggested somebody had looked it up too, made the whole thing sound official, an ecosystem with edges and rules. What she cared about was the schedule. Same day, every week, same faces, three hours of picking up trash along the bank with people who would have to keep seeing her until seeing her became normal.

The first Thursday, she counted. Two hours of actual work, maybe, once you subtracted the sign-in sheet and the break. She stood in the shallows pulling a bicycle tire out of the reeds while a boy named only in her head as Tall Guy With The Clipboard asked her where she'd moved from, and she told him, and he said the drive was brutal, and that was the entire conversation. Ninety hours. She waded back to shore with the tire over her shoulder like a donut of garbage and thought about how Ariel would have already made three jokes about it.

She texted Ariel that night from the floor of her room, on a sleeping bag, because the mattress was still in the truck in Florida somewhere. "Update from the machination front," she wrote. "I have engineered a scheme to acquire friends through mandatory weekly proximity. The scheme involves a river." Ariel sent back a row of crying-laughing faces and then, a minute later, "wait you actually joined something? you hate joining things." "I hate starting from zero more," Payton wrote, and after she sent it she stared at it, because it was true and also not the whole truth. She didn't hate starting from zero. She was afraid of it, which was different, and she hadn't figured out yet whether the fear or the plan was going to win.

Ms. Mercer ran the club, a retired science teacher who brought thermoses of coffee and never asked anyone why they'd come. On the fourth Thursday, when rain cut the cleanup short, she gathered everyone under the pavilion and passed out cups, and Payton found herself standing between Tall Guy With The Clipboard, whose name turned out to be Sam, no, whose name was not allowed to be Sam, there were no other names she was keeping, and a girl who interposed herself into the conversation about the weird tire Payton had found, saying, "Wait, was that the one with the seaweed in it? My brother has a theory it belonged to a ghost." Payton said the ghost should file a claim. The girl laughed so hard she spilled her coffee.

Walking back to the car, damp and smelling of river, Payton did the arithmetic again. Twelve hours, maybe fifteen with the rain delay and the pavilion. She was allowed to text Ariel now without checking first, and she did: "15 down." Ariel replied with a photo of the two of them from graduation, and the words "75 to go on your end. 0 on mine." Payton sat in the driver's seat for a while before starting the engine, the windshield fogging around the edges. Then she typed, "same time next thursday," and drove home to the empty house, where her mattress had finally arrived and was leaning against the wall of her room like a door to somewhere.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The line outside the community hall stretched past the folding tables where the brownies usually sat on bake-sale Saturdays, and Matthew stood in it with his registration card going soft in his hand. His eighteenth birthday had been eleven days earlier, which meant that today, for the first time in his life, someone would actually have to count him. Behind him, Luka was reading the ballot preview on his phone with the solemn expression of a man defusing a bomb.

"You've changed your mind four times since the parking lot," Luka said without looking up. "I'm keeping a tally."

"I've changed it twice. The other two were lateral moves." Matthew had spent the drive listening to his father, who believed a vote was a chess piece, a thing you sacrificed for position, and then to Heaven in the passenger seat, who believed a vote was a signature, a thing you wrote in your own hand or not at all. Both arguments had arrived intact and neither had left. Heaven had gone inside already, early riser that she were, and the sliding doors opened and shut behind the queue like a slow argument with the weather.

The hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. A woman at the check-in table found his name, crossed it off with a ruler-straight stroke, and directed him toward the second voting screen, the one with the wobbly leg. It was there, waiting his turn behind a man in a crepuscular cardigan who took an unreasonably long time folding his ballot, that Matthew asked the question he'd been carrying since the parking lot. "Do you know how long people my age have been able to do this? It feels like it should be, I don't know, forever."

The cardigan man shuffled off toward the box. Luka, who had followed him up despite not being able to vote until next year, a fact he mentioned roughly every nine minutes, shook his head. "You think it's ancient. It's not. Canada lowered the federal voting age from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970. That's it. That's the whole history."

"Nineteen seventy." Matthew did the arithmetic twice, the way he did it for exams, because the first answer seemed wrong. "That's my dad's lifetime. Barely." He had been imagining some crepuscular, misty origin, premiers in whiskers, an eternity of eighteen-year-olds trooping to the polls, and instead the whole tradition was younger than the carpet in this hall. Something about that shifted the weight of the card in his hand. If the door had only been open since 1970, then people had pushed it open, which meant it had once seemed as impossible as Luka voting now, which meant the chess-piece theory and the signature theory were both, somehow, arguments people had been having since before either of his parents could drive.

Behind the screen, the ballot offered him three names and a fourth he'd never heard of, whose platform appeared to consist entirely of a promise to expiate the nation's sins through compulsory poetry. Matthew stood there longer than was strictly necessary. His father's voice said, in memory, that a vote wasted on conscience is a vote donated to the other side. Heaven's voice said, in memory, that if you can't sign your own name you shouldn't sign anything. He thought about 1970, about how every arrangement he'd ever been told was permanent turned out, on inspection, to have a start date, and he marked the ballot for the candidate he actually wanted, the one polling at six percent, the one his father called a rounding error.

Then he stood in front of the box, ballot in hand, and did not put it in.

The cardigan man was long gone. A poll worker was pretending not to watch him. Luka leaned against the wall near the exit, grinning, already composing the tally. Matthew looked down at his folded ballot, the little crease he'd made in it, and felt the honest thing, which was that he did not know whether he'd just done something principled or something his grandfather would have called decorating. Both readings were available. Neither closed the other out.

He dropped the ballot in, heard the soft wooden sound of it landing, and went to find Heaven, who was waiting by the bake-sale tables with two day-old brownies and a look of unbearable patience.

"So?" she said.

"I signed my name," Matthew said. "Probably."

Luka held out his hand. "That'll be four changes of mind. I believe you owe me a brownie."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The wind came off the parking lot in gusts, and every gust took Alexis's cap and tried to keep it. He caught it twice before it reached the hedges, and the second time Daniella laughed so hard she had to lean on Marilou's shoulder to stay upright in her heels.

"Hold it down," Marilou said, which was not advice anyone could use. All three of them had the caps on because Ms. Banerjee had told them to wear them to the restaurant, since her reservation was under "Party of Eight, Graduation," and she wanted the staff to know what they were celebrating. Alexis suspected she also wanted the caps visible from the road.

The reservation was for eight fifteen. It was seven fifty-two, and the walk from the lot to the door took about a minute, so there was no reason to hurry, and yet the three of them hurried, which was the kind of thing people did on days that had already decided their shape. Alexis had been sensitized, over four years of lunches at the same table, to the exact pitch of Daniella's laughter, and this pitch meant she was happy, not covering for anything, and he was glad about that in a way he did not say out loud.

"Why is it like this, though?" Daniella said, holding her own cap down with one hand while pulling the door with the other. "A square hat. Whoever decided a square hat was the thing."

"Beats me," Alexis said.

"It has a name," Marilou said. "I know it has a name. I heard it at rehearsal and now it's gone."

Inside, the restaurant smelled of garlic and scorched butter, and the hostess led them past a table of adults in office clothes to the long table in the back where Ms. Banerjee was already sitting with a glass of water she had not touched, correcting the place settings one fork at a time. The other five seats filled within minutes: the boy from Alexis's physics class, two girls whose names Alexis had never learned in four years, and a girl who had transferred in February and knew no one, which Ms. Banerjee had apparently decided to fix by seating her directly across from Alexis.

What Alexis could not have said, from where he sat, was that the February girl, whose name was also, improbably, Daniella, had spent the whole ceremony being informed by the first Daniella that there was now a system of nicknames. But the narrator has moved across the table now, into the second Daniella's seat, from which Alexis appears as a boy holding a phone under the table like a criminal, and from which the first Daniella appears as a force of weather.

"Alexis," Ms. Banerjee said. "The phone."

"It's for the hat," Alexis said, and turned the screen toward her. He had found it while everyone was ordering, in the gap between the spring rolls and the pho, because Marilou had refused to let the name go and he could not stand a question sitting unanswered in the middle of a table. "It's called a mortarboard," he read. "Because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar."

There was a pause while everyone at the table absorbed this, and then the first Daniella put her cap on the table, square and flat and slightly dented from the hedges, and looked at it as if it were suddenly a different object, which in a sense it was. The February Daniella reached over and turned it so the tassel hung off the edge like a plumb line. "So we've all been wearing construction equipment," she said.

"On our heads," Marilou said. "For four hours."

Ms. Banerjee, who had watched the entire exchange with the expression of someone awaiting an acquittal she was fairly confident about, lifted her water glass a centimeter and then set it back down. "The food is coming," she said. "Hats off the table."

The hats went onto the bench and the backs of chairs, and Alexis made a judicious retreat from the phone to his napkin, since the pho was arriving and pho did not wait. He was thinking, though he would not have phrased it this way even if someone had asked, that there were two ways to hold the evening: as the end of something, which the caps kept insisting on, or as a square flat thing with a name he had not known this morning and would remember for no reason, the way a bricklayer's board holds mortar until it becomes a wall. He did not know which way he would remember it. The February Daniella passed him the lime, and he took it.

fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Gavin found the voter information card on the kitchen table with his name spelled slightly wrong, which was strange, because the card belonged to his mother. He turned it over twice, checked the return address, and finally understood: his own card had never come. He was eighteen, it was federal election day, and he had never registered. The polling station opened at seven and closed at seven-thirty, and between those hours he had school, a shift at the grocery store, and, apparently, a civic problem.

He texted Kobe first, because Kobe had turned eighteen in November and voted in the advance polls like a small-town celebrity. "did u register or does it just happen," Gavin typed, then added, "asking for me." Kobe's answer came back as a shrug emoji and "think u register when u do taxes???" which was the kind of information that raised more questions than it settled. Gavin sat on the stairs with his toast going cold and wondered how a whole system could run on paperwork he'd never been told about. Didn't the school do something? Had there been a form, some beige announcement he'd recycled without reading?

Faris picked up on the second ring. "My dad says you show up and they deal with you there," Faris said, mouth clearly full of something. "He's very confident, but he's also confident the Leafs will win the Cup, so calibrate accordingly." Gavin said thanks anyway and hung up, no wiser. He looked down the street toward the elementary school that served as his polling place, four blocks of wet pavement under a sky the grey of dishwater, the last of the boreal cold still clinging to the morning. The poll had been open for an hour already. People were walking toward it with the unhurried certainty of those who had received mail.

Ms. Chen was sweeping her front walk three houses down, as she did every morning regardless of weather, a virtuoso of the broom who could clear a sidewalk the way others played piano. Gavin had known her since he was seven and had once, memorably, helped her resuscitate a drowning bee with sugar water, an operation she had supervised with clinical seriousness. He asked her the question straight out, because she was the only adult he knew who answered questions instead of asking three back.

"If you're not on the voters list, you can register at your polling place on election day," she said, leaning on the broom. "Bring ID with your address. Bring proof of address. Bring patience." She did not say this like a lesson. She said it the way she said rain was coming, a fact of the atmosphere.

He went home for his passport, his bank statement, his hydro bill folded into thirds, and he walked to the school trying to hold two thoughts at once without letting either flatten the other. His mother, who had campaigned in her twenties for a party he disagreed with now, had taught him that voting was a duty so basic it needed no argument. Kobe, who had read three books about electoral reform out of pure boredom, argued that a single vote was statistically weightless and that pretending otherwise was a kind of theatre. Gavin had always drifted between them, borrowing conviction from his mother when he wanted to feel like part of something and borrowing Kobe's arithmetic when he wanted to feel smart. He noticed, walking, that he was doing it again right now, and that noticing it didn't make choosing easier.

The gym smelled of floor wax and juice boxes. A woman at a folding table looked up his address, pointed him to the registration desk, and a man with a lanyard copied his documents onto a form while a line formed behind him, patient and faintly annoyed. The ballot was handed over folded, and behind the cardboard screen Gavin stood for a long moment with his pencil. It occurred to him that he had spent more energy on getting here than on deciding how to mark the paper, which seemed backwards, though he couldn't quite say whether that made the marking less meaningful or more. He made his X, refolded the sheet, and slid it into the box just as another voter's slid in beside it, indistinguishable, both of them gone.

Outside, Faris called to ask if he'd been turned away. "I got on the list," Gavin said. "They sorted it right there." He stood by the bike racks watching the steady trickle of people going in, each carrying some private version of the same decision, none of them visible in the box afterward. He didn't know yet whether his side would win, or whether winning would mean what he hoped, and he found he could carry not-knowing more easily than he'd expected. His phone buzzed: his shift started in twenty minutes. He zipped his jacket and started toward the store.
